en: Arjuna said:
What is that Brahman? What is the inner self (adhyātma)? What is action, O Supreme Person?
And what is declared to be the "with respect to the elements" (adhibhūta), and what is called the "with respect to the divine" (adhidaiva)? //1//
Śrīdhara:
"Those whose minds are fixed on Kṛṣṇa alone know Brahman, karma, the presiding deities, and so forth.
Having thus mentioned Brahman, karma, and the rest, they are now clearly explained in the eighth [chapter].

At the end of the previous chapter, Arjuna, desiring to know the true nature of the seven categories—beginning with Brahman and the Adhyātma—which were introduced by the Blessed One, spoke in two verses beginning with "What is that Brahman?
The meaning is clear. (1)

Madhusūdana: At the end of the preceding chapter, with the half-verse beginning "They know that Brahman, the whole of the Adhyātma, and all Karma," the Blessed One provided a summary (sūtra) of the seven categories as objects of knowledge; this eighth chapter, which serves as a commentary (vṛtti) upon them, is now commenced.
Therein, desiring to understand specifically the seven topics set forth in the aphorisms, [the author] speaks in two verses:
Is that Brahman which is said to be "knowable" possessed of adjuncts (*sopādhika*) or devoid of adjuncts (*nirupādhika*)?

Likewise, with respect to the body as the self (*adhyātma*), does that which "abides in that substratum" refer to the collection of instruments such as the ears, or to the inwardly directed consciousness (*pratyak-caitanya*)?

Regarding the phrase "likewise all action," one might wonder whether "action" refers to that which is of the nature of sacrifice or something else, since the Śruti declares two kinds: "He performs the sacrifice of knowledge and also performs actions.
Dispelling the doubt as to why You ask me this—given that You and I are equal—the address "O Puruṣottama" indicates that for You, who are the Supreme Person and omniscient, there is nothing unknown.

And what is declared to be *adhibhūta*? Does the term *adhibhūta* intend to refer to any effect whatsoever with respect to the elements such as earth, or does it refer to the entire aggregate of effects?
The word *ca* (and) serves to collect all these questions together.
And what is called *adhidaiva*: is it meditation directed toward the deities, or is it the consciousness permeating all deities, such as the solar orb and the rest? //1//
Viśvanātha: In the eighth [chapter], [the Lord] spoke in response to Arjuna’s question regarding Yoga, mixed devotion, and— incidentally— pure devotion, as well as the two destinies.
At the end of the previous chapter, the Blessed One spoke of the knowledge of the seven categories beginning with Brahmā.
Here, desiring to know their true nature, he asks in two verses:
"In this body, who is the adhiyajña, the presiding deity of sacrifice?"
And how that [Self] is to be known within this body is the subject to be followed by the subsequent [section]. //1-2//
Baladeva:
Being questioned by Utkala, Hari sequentially explained Brahmā and the others in the eighth chapter,
as well as the two paths of devotion— both that mixed with yoga and that which is pure.
At the end of the preceding chapter, Arjuna asks in order to understand the seven categories beginning with Brahman, which were designated as objects to be known by those seeking liberation:

"What is that Brahman? Does it mean the consciousness of the Supreme Self (paramātma-caitanya), or does it mean the consciousness of the individual self (jīvātma-caitanya)? This is the meaning of the question.
Regarding the term *adhyātma*, according to its etymology (*nirukti*), it means "with reference to the self" (*ātman*) or the body;
or else, it refers to the collection of the sense organs beginning with hearing, or the collection of the subtle elements.
The address "O Puruṣottama" is used to dispel the doubt: "Since we two are equal [in this regard], why do you ask me?"—thereby removing that apprehension.
The sense is: "Because you are the Supreme Lord, everything is well known to you, but not to me.

What is the *adhibhūta*? According to the etymology "that which presides over (*adhikṛtya*) the elements (*bhūtāni*)," it is either the products such as a pot or the gross body. What is the *adhidaiva*? It is either meditation directed toward the deities or the cosmic aggregate, the Virāṭ. //1//
O Madhusūdana, who is the Lord of Sacrifice here in this body, and how? And at the time of departure, how are You to be known by those of self-restraint? (8.2)
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, regarding the phrase "adhiyajña" (the presiding deity of sacrifice): in this body, what is the presiding deity (*adhiṣṭhātā*) over the sacrifice that is performed?
The meaning is: who is the instigator and the giver of the fruit?
Having asked about his own nature, he now asks about the manner of his presiding: "How"—by what mode—"does he abide" in this body, meaning how does he preside over the sacrifice?
The mention of "sacrifice" (yajña) is intended as an illustration for all ritual actions.
And at the time of death, by what means are you to be known by persons whose minds are disciplined? //2//

Madhusūdana: Adhiyajña is the deity-soul who has entered into the sacrifice, or the Supreme Brahman. And how, in what manner, is he to be meditated upon? Is it through identity (*tādātmya*), or rather through absolute non-difference (*atyantābheda*)?
In any case, does he exist within this body or outside of it?
If he is within the body, is he the intellect and so forth, or is he distinct from them? How and who is the "adhiyajña" here? Thus, there are not two questions.
However, it should be understood that there is only one question, though presented in various forms.

Addressing him as "O Madhusūdana," he indicates that since the Blessed One is supremely compassionate and removes all calamities even with effort, it is entirely appropriate and easy for him to remove the calamity caused by my affection without any exertion.

And at the time of departure, because all the faculties are distracted and mental concentration is impossible, how—in what manner—are You to be known by those of self-restraint with concentrated minds? The particle *ca* (and) is intended to indicate this aforementioned doubt.
The underlying intention is: "Please tell all of this to me, who have come for refuge, because of Your omniscience and supreme compassion. //2//
Viśvanātha: [nothing].
Baladeva: "Who is the Adhiyajña? means: is it Indra and the others who preside over the sacrifice, or is it Viṣṇu?
"How? means: in what way does he possess the status of being the Adhiyajña?
The address "O Madhusūdana" is intended to make it known to you that all of this removal of my doubt is easy for you;
the meaning is that at the time of departure (*prayāṇa*), because of the distraction of all the senses, the concentration of the mind is impossible. //2//
The Blessed Lord said:
The imperishable, supreme Brahman is called the Self (adhyātma) as its own nature.
The emission that brings about the origin of the existence of beings is designated as action (karman). //3//
Śrīdhara: In accordance with the sequence of questions, the Blessed Lord spoke the answer in three verses beginning with "the Imperishable" (akṣara).
It is called *akṣara* because it does not perish (*kṣarati*) nor does it move (*calati*). Now, one might object: is not the individual soul (*jīva*) also imperishable?
That which is the supreme imperishable (akṣara), the root cause of the world, is Brahman. For the Śruti declares: "O Gārgī, the Brāhmaṇas indeed call this the imperishable.
Its inherent nature (svabhāva) is to exist in the form of the individual soul (jīva) as a partial manifestation (aṃśa) of that very Brahman itself.
The meaning is that this very [Self], existing as the enjoyer with reference to the body, is designated by the term *adhyātma*.
The "existence" (*bhāva*) of beings—such as those born from a womb and so forth—is their birth (*utpatti*).
And "emergence" (*udbhava*) is their coming into being in a superior state (*utkṛṣṭatvena bhavanam*).
An oblation properly cast into the fire reaches the sun;
from the sun rain is born, from rain comes food, and from that, living beings.
Thus is the gradual increase.

That emission (*visarga*) which brings about the manifestation of those two—the past and the future—is sacrifice (*yajña*), consisting of the relinquishment of material objects for the sake of the deity;
this is an illustration of all ritual actions, and it is denoted by the word "action" (*karman*). //3//
Madhusūdana: Thus, the answers to the seven questions are given in sequence by means of three verses.

With the intention that the fulfillment of the questioner's desire may occur effortlessly when the determination follows the order of the questions, the Blessed Lord has here determined three questions in sequence within this verse.
Likewise, there is a division such that there are three questions in the second verse and one in the third verse.

He provides the answer to the first question—that by the word "Brahman" it is Brahman without attributes (*nirupādhika*) that is intended here, and not Brahman with attributes (*sopādhika*)—as follows: "The Imperishable (*akṣara*)," meaning that which does not perish or is indestructible, or else that which pervades all, being all-pervasive.
"This indeed, O Gārgī, is that Imperishable which the Brāhmaṇas declare," beginning with [the description] "neither gross nor subtle," and so forth.

"By the command of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, the sun and the moon stand held apart; there is no other seer than this," and so on—having thus referred to it in the middle, the Śruti concludes: "In this very Imperishable, O Gārgī, the ether is woven like warp and woof."
It is empty of all adjuncts, the ruler of all,
the sustainer of the entire phenomenal world extending to the unmanifested ether;
and it is the knower within this aggregate of body and senses.
Unconditioned consciousness (caitanya) is what is intended here by the term "Brahman.
He explains this very point with the word "supreme" (paramam):

it is supreme because its nature consists of self-luminosity and supreme bliss, and because the marks of governance—the sustaining of the entire aggregate of insentient things—are logically possible only therein.
This is because of the principle [stated in Brahma Sūtra 1.3.10]: "The Imperishable [is Brahman], because it supports everything up to the ether.

However, in this context, since the word *akṣara* is conventionally established (*rūḍhi*) as referring merely to a phoneme (*varṇa*), the conventional meaning takes precedence over the etymological meaning (*yoga*) according to the principle that "convention overrides etymology" based on the logic of the section concerning the indicative marks of the Śruti regarding the *rathakāra*. Thus, it refers to the syllable known as *praṇava*, just as the term *rathakāra* denotes a specific caste.
In that context, the syllable itself (*akṣara*) is what should be grasped, because the indicative mark (*liṅga*) mentioned therein is possible [only for it];

and because of the subsequent qualification, "The single-syllabled *om* is Brahman," according to the maxim: "For those whose purpose is obstructed by another meaning, the relative strength and weakness are reversed.

However, in the case of the statement, "A chariot-maker (*rathakāra*) should perform the fire-consecration during the rains," the distinction is that there is no impossibility regarding a specific caste (*jāti*).
However, the sublation of *śruti* by a mark (*liṅga*) that cannot be established otherwise has been explained in such passages as "ākāśa [is Brahman] because of its mark" and so forth.
But here, this much is the distinction:
when there is a sublation of *śruti* by a mark that cannot be established otherwise, if a figurative application (*yoga*) is possible, that alone is accepted because of its primacy (*mukhyatva*).
As in "they praise with the *ājya* [stotras]" and "they praise with the *pṛṣṭha* [stotras]," and as in the word *akṣara* in this very context;
but where even such etymological derivation (*yoga*) is not possible, there the function is metaphorical (*gauṇī vṛtti*), as in the words *ākāśa*, *prāṇa*, and so forth.
If it is argued that even for the word "ākāśa," the etymological derivation (yoga)— namely, "that which shines forth (kāśate) completely (ā) [everywhere] within Brahman"— is possible,
then let that very derivation be accepted; so says the author of the Pañcapādī.
And likewise: "The Sūtra on the consideration [of the meaning], and because of its well-known status" (Vs 1.3.17).
Enough has been said here in detail.
Thus, it has been determined what that Brahman is.
Now, it is determined what "adhyātma" (the inner self) is.

That which was called the imperishable Brahman—its very nature (*svabhāva*), its own being (*svo bhāvaḥ*), its essential form (*svarūpa*), is the inward consciousness (*pratyak-cetanya*); however, it is not a genitive compound meaning "the state of one's own" (*svasya bhāvaḥ*), because that would entail the fault of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

Because the adoption of the *karmadhāraya* compound— by overriding the *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuru�șa*— is established by the *Viṣada-sthapati* section through the connection of the meanings of the words as they are heard [in the text], [the term "adhyātma"] does not refer to that which is related to Brahman, but rather to the very nature of Brahman itself. The meaning is that the word "adhyātma" denotes that which exists as the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*) with reference to the body (*ātman*), and not the collection of instruments (*karaṇa-grāma*).
In response to the third question, he states that by the word "action" (*karma*) here, only Vedic action consisting of sacrifice (*yāga*), gift-giving (*dāna*), and oblation (*homa*) is intended;

for it is that renunciation (*visarga*)— prescribed by the scriptures and consisting of sacrifice, gift-giving, and oblation— which effects the being (*bhāva*), the birth, and the growth of all beings (*bhūtānām*), that is, of all things characterized by coming into existence, whether stationary or moving.
Here, it is designated as "action" (*karman*);
that is to say, it is expressed by the word *karman*.

Among these, a sacrifice (*yāga*) is the relinquishment of a substance intended for a deity; it begins with the act of rising and ends with the employment of the *vaṣaṭ*-call. It is also called an oblation (*homa*).
That very same *upaviṣṭahoma* is a sacrifice that concludes with the utterance of *svāhā* and extends up to the final pouring of water;
whereas *dāna* (giving) is the relinquishment of ownership that extends until the acquisition of ownership by another.
And in every case, the element of relinquishment (*tyāga*) is present.
And its capacity to produce the manifestation of existing things is established by the traditional teaching (smṛti): "An oblation properly cast into the fire reaches the sun;
from the sun rain is born; from rain comes food; and from that, living beings."
And because of such scriptural passages as: "These two oblations, when offered, depart," and so forth. //3//
Viśvanātha says: He gives the answer with the word "akṣaram" (the Imperishable).
That which does not perish is the "akṣara," the eternal; that which is supreme is Brahman—according to the Śruti: "O Gārgī, the Brāhmaṇas declare this indeed to be that Imperishable.
"Svabhāva" is the individual soul (jīva), so called because it brings about or generates its own self through the power of superimposing [the notion of] a body upon itself.

Alternatively, that which causes one's own [nature] to manifest and leads one to the Supreme Self is *svabhāva*; this refers to the pure soul (*śuddha-jīva*), which is called "the internal" (*adhyātma*).
The meaning is that it is denoted by the term *adhyātma*.

That which brings about the emergence of entities—namely, human bodies and so forth—by means of the elements alone is *visarga*, the transmigratory cycle of the soul; because it is produced by karma, it is designated as "karma."
The meaning is that by the word "karma," the transmigratory existence of the individual soul (jīva) is expressed. //3//

Baladeva: Thus questioned, the Blessed One gave the answer to the seven questions in sequence, beginning with "the Imperishable" (*akṣara*). By its etymology, "that which does not perish" (*na kṣarati*), it is the Imperishable—the supreme consciousness of the individual self (*jīvātman*) distinct from the body and so forth. That is what I call Brahman. Its designation as "Imperishable" and as "Brahman" is established by the following scriptural knowledge: "The unmanifest dissolves into the Imperishable; the Imperishable dissolves into darkness; darkness becomes one in the Supreme. And: "If one knows Brahman as Consciousness..."
Thus it is stated in the Śruti.
Regarding the term "svabhāva" (intrinsic nature):
it refers to that entity (bhāva) related to one's own individual self (jīvātman), characterized by the subtle elements (bhūta-sūkṣma) and their latent impressions (vāsanā).

Because it is recited in the *pañcāgni-vidyā* and is connected to that [individual] self (*ātman*), it is called "internal" (*adhyātma*) by me. "Existence" (*bhūta*) refers to the state of those subtle elements when they are conjoined with their gross forms, characterized as humans and so forth; the "emission" (*visarga*) which causes their emergence—that is, their production—is designated as "action" (*karman*).

Having attained heaven through rituals such as the *jyotiṣṭoma*, and having experienced that [heaven] with a divine body, one remains with the residue of experience, like the remainder of ghee transferred from a vessel.
That residue of karma which is discharged for the sake of obtaining a body as a human being or other such forms on earth is called "karma" by me.

In the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*, five oblations—faith (*śraddhā*), soma, rain, food, and semen—are taught in sequence as being offered into five fires: those of heaven, the rain-cloud, the earth, man, and woman.
The meaning therein is this: the Vedic soul offers oblations of curd and other substances with faith in this world.

Those waters, consisting of curd and other substances, being composed of the five elements through the process of quintuplication (pañcīkaraṇa), remain connected to that living soul in the form of the oblation called "faith" (śraddhā) because they were offered with faith.
Then, when he has died, the deities who preside over his sense organs offer them as an oblation into the fire of the heavenly world (dyuloka).
The meaning is that they lead the individual soul (jīva), endowed with those [elements], to heaven.
Once offered, those elements transform into a divine body known as the "Soma-king"; with that body, he experiences the fruits of his karma there.
At the conclusion of that enjoyment, the soul, together with those bodies, being offered by the gods into the fire of Parjanya, becomes rain.

Having become rain, those [beings] together with their life-principle (jīva) are offered into the fire of the earth by them and attain the state of food such as rice; having become food, those [beings] together with their life-principle are offered into the fire of man and partake of the state of semen;

having become semen, those [beings] together with their life-principle are offered into the fire of woman by them and, existing in the form of an embryo, proceed to the state of a human being. Thus, the cause for attaining that state is the remainder of karma denoted by the term "latent tendency" (anuśaya).
Regarding "action" (*karman*): this has been stated by the author of the Sūtras in such passages as "in the practice immediately following that," and so forth. //3//
The perishable state is the *adhibhūta* (the field of material elements), and the *puruṣa* (the individual soul) is the *adhidaivata* (the field of the presiding deity).
I alone am the *adhiyajña* (the field of sacrifice) here in this body, O best among the embodied. 8.4.
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, regarding the term *adhibhūta*:
the perishable (*kṣara*) is the transitory entity, such as the body and other objects;
it is called *adhibhūta* because it exists with reference to (*adhikṛtya*) all living beings (*bhūta*).
The Vairāja Puruṣa, who resides in the center of the solar orb and is the sovereign lord of all deities who are his own partial manifestations, is called the *adhidaivata*.
The *adhidaivata* is the presiding deity.
He is indeed the first embodied being; he is called the Puruṣa.
"From the Vedic scripture: 'He is the first creator of beings; Brahmā appeared in the beginning.
Here, in this body, I alone, abiding as the inner controller (antaryāmin), am the Adhiyajña—the initiator of rituals such as sacrifice and the bestower of their fruits.
How so? The answer to this must also be understood from this very [scripture]."
Because it is well known that the Inner Controller (antaryāmin) exists within the body by virtue of qualities such as non-attachment, which distinguish Him from the individual soul (jīva);
and thus says the Śruti:
"Two birds, inseparable companions..."
They both embrace the same tree;
one of them eats the sweet fruit, while the other looks on without eating. (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.1)

By addressing you as "the best among embodied beings," he indicates that you too ought to understand such an Inner Controller (antaryāmin) through the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) of your own activities and cessations being dependent upon another. //4//
Madhusūdana: Now he provides the answer to the next three questions with the word "adhibhūtam.

That which perishes is "kṣara," meaning perishable; whatever entity possesses birth is a "bhūta," a class of living beings. That which exists presiding over these is called "adhibhūta. The Puruṣa is Hiraṇyagarbha, the collective subtle body (*samaṣṭi-liṅga-ātman*), the sustainer of all individual organs (*vyaṣṭi-sarva-karaṇa*), who [is described as] "this was indeed the Self in the beginning."

Beginning with the passage, "He was in the form of a person," it is established by such scriptural texts as, "Because he burnt (auṣat) all evils prior to this entire universe, therefore he is called 'Puruṣa'"; and by the word "and" (ca), [it is further supported by] the statement:
"He is indeed the first embodied one; he is indeed called Puruṣa."
He was the first creator of beings; as Brahmā, he existed at the beginning.
This is also established by such Smṛti passages as these.
With respect to the divine (*adhidaivata*), he presides over the deities, such as the Sun and others, thereby favoring the instruments of perception, such as the eyes.
Likewise, he is called *adhiyajña*, the presiding deity of all sacrifices and the bestower of the fruits of all sacrifices.
The deity presiding over all sacrifices, known as Viṣṇu— according to the Vedic revelation, "Viṣṇu is indeed sacrifice"—
is that very Viṣṇu who is I, Vāsudeva, and not anyone distinct from me.
Therefore, it has been explained how He is to be understood as being absolutely non-different from the Supreme Brahman.
And He exists here within this human body in the form of sacrifice, being distinct from the intellect and other faculties because His nature is that of Viṣṇu.

By this, the doubt is dispelled as to whether He is in this body or outside of it; for if He were in the body, one might wonder whether He is the intellect and so forth, or something distinct from them.
Furthermore, the abiding of sacrifice in the human body is due to the fact that sacrifice is accomplished by means of the human body.
"The sacrifice is indeed the person; by means of the person is the sacrifice [performed], because the person extends it"—so says the Śruti.

Addressing Arjuna as "O best among embodied beings," meaning the foremost of all living creatures, the Blessed Lord encourages him, saying: "By conversing with Me at every moment, you have fulfilled your purpose and are now fit to understand this."
Arjuna’s status as the foremost among all living beings is indeed well known, owing to his being the recipient of the supreme grace of the Blessed Lord. //4//

Viśvanātha: The perishable (*kṣara*), which is the transitory entity or object such as a pot or a cloth, is designated by the term *adhibhūta*. The Person (*puruṣa*)—the collective Virāṭ—is designated by the term *adhidaivata*, according to its etymological derivation as "that in which the presiding deities such as the Sun and others exist. Here, within this body, I am the *adhiyajña*, the inner controller (*antaryāmī*) who impels actions such as sacrifice; because He is a portion of Me, it is I alone.

Regarding the question "How is He to be known?", the answer given by the word *eva* (indeed) is this: in His capacity as the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*), He is to be known as non-different from Me; the meaning is that He is not to be known as different from Me in the manner of the individual self (*adhyātman*) and so forth.
By the phrase "in the body, O best among embodied beings," the intention is that you, however, because you are My direct friend, are indeed the most excellent of all. //4//
Baladeva: "Adhīti.
A perishable entity (*kṣara*) that undergoes transformation at every moment, namely the gross body, is called by me *adhibhūta*.
This is because of the etymological derivation: that which exists (*bhavati*) with reference to (*adhikṛtya*) a living being (*bhūta*).
The Puruṣa who is the collective Virāṭ is called by me "the presiding deity" (*adhidaiva*), based on the etymology that he exists presiding over the deities such as Āditya and others.
Here, in this body, I alone am the "presiding sacrifice" (*adhiyajña*), based on the etymology that He exists presiding over the sacrifice; I am both its initiator and the bestower of its fruit.
As for the things to be rejected, they should be inferred by oneself.
By the word *eva*, its difference from itself is excluded.

By this [word], the answer to the question "How? has also been stated: the meaning is that, by internally restricting [myself] through having a body the size of a span (*prādeśa-mātra-vapuṣ*), I am the instigator of sacrifices and other rites.
And thus, by serving my worship (*mad-arcā*), one finds these seven objects, beginning with Brahmā, in their true nature without effort.
In that context, Brahman and the sacrifice are to be attained, whereas the internal [self] and so forth are to be abandoned. //4//
And at the time of death, he who departs casting off the body while remembering Me alone attains My state; there is no doubt about this. (8.5)

Śrīdhara: By the words "and at the time of departure, you shall be known," [the Lord] shows the means of knowledge and its fruit for the final moment. Regarding the verse beginning with "at the final moment":

he who, remembering Me alone—the Supreme Lord in the form of the Inner Controller as previously described—casts off the body and proceeds by the excellent path of the northern course via the route of light (*arcis*) and so forth, attains My state, that is, My own nature.
There is no doubt in this matter: remembrance is the means to knowledge, and the attainment of my own state is the fruit; such is the meaning. //5//

Madhusūdana says: He now provides the answer to the seventh question—“How are You to be known at the time of departure?”—in the verse beginning with “And at the time of death. One who, at the time of death, remembers Me alone—the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva, the Adhiyajña, whether as possessing attributes (saguṇa) or devoid of them (nirguṇa), the Supreme Imperishable Brahman, and not merely the Adhyātma and so forth—constantly contemplates Him; by the intensity of that mental impression, even while possessed of the distraction of the entire aggregate of the senses, [he attains Me].
Even at the time of death, he who departs— having abandoned the body and relinquished the egoistic and possessive notions of "I" and "mine" regarding the physical frame—
travels by way of the path of the gods (*devayāna*), as will be described in the passage beginning with "fire, light, day, the bright fortnight," and so forth; this practitioner,
excelling over the path of the ancestors (*pitṛyāna*), attains my state, that is, my own nature, which is the state of the attributeless Brahman.
At the end of the enjoyment of the world of Hiraṇyagarbha, he goes—that is, he attains it.

However, in the case of the recollection of the attributeless Brahman (nirguṇa-brahma), the phrase "having abandoned the body, he departs" refers to the perspective of worldly convention; for according to the Śruti, "his vital breaths do not depart, they are merged right here," there is no departure of his vital breaths, and thus, due to the absence of such departure, there is no going.
"He goes directly to My state; being Brahman, he attains Brahman" (BAU 4.4.6)—according to this scripture.
There is no doubt here regarding the Self as distinct from the body, nor regarding the attainment of My state. [The question remains:
is the Self distinct from the body and so forth, or not?

Even regarding the soul's distinction from the body, there is no doubt as to whether it is different from the Lord or not, according to the Śruti: "All doubts are cut away" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.8). In this context, it should be understood that by the statement "having abandoned the physical frame, he departs," the soul's difference from the body is stated; and by the statement "he attains my state," its non-difference from the Lord is stated. //5//
Viśvanātha: He provides the answer to the question, "How are You to be known at the time of departure? with the words, "And at the time of death...
"Remembering Me alone" means that the remembrance of Me is itself the knowledge of Me;
the sense is that, unlike a jar or a cloth, I cannot be known in reality by anyone [in the same manner].
The modes of knowledge in the form of recollection will be explained in the fourteenth verse. //5//
Baladeva: He provides the answer to the question, "How are You to be known at the time of departure? with the verse beginning with *ante*.

Here, it is stated that by being known through knowledge consisting of remembrance, one attains my state (*mad-bhāva*), and I grant that as its fruit. In this context, "my state" (*mad-bhāva*) means my own essential nature (*mat-svabhāva*).
Just as I am by nature distinguished by the eightfold qualities such as freedom from evil, so too shall he who remembers me become like that. //5//
Whatever state of being one remembers when leaving the body at the end,
to that very state one goes, O son of Kuntī, having been constantly absorbed in that state.
Śrīdhara: It is not the rule that one attains my own state merely by remembering me.

What then? "Whichever... and so forth. Whatever state—whether another deity or something else—one remembers at the time of death while leaving the body, one attains that very state which was being remembered.
At the time of death, the cause for the recollection of a particular state is "always being permeated by that state.
This means that at all times, his state—namely, cultivation (*bhāvanā*), which is constant reflection—is present; he is "permeated" by that, meaning his mind has been infused with it. //6//

Madhusūdana: To show that for one who meditates upon the Blessed One at the time of death, the attainment of the Blessed One is certain, [the Lord] says "yaṃ yaṃ" (whichever), indicating that for anyone else who meditates on anything whatsoever at that time and abandons the body, the attainment of that very thing is inevitable.
It is not the rule that one attains my own state merely by remembering me; rather, whatever state— be it a particular deity or,
by the force of the word "ca," anything else whatsoever— one remembers or contemplates at the end, at the time of casting off the body upon the departure of the vital breaths,
one attains and reaches that very remembered state and none other.
By addressing him as "O son of Kuntī," he indicates an excess of affection due to being the son of his paternal aunt;
by that [affection], he implies that [Arjuna] must necessarily be favored, and by that, the absence of any suspicion of deception.
He states this because even when the effort of recollection is impossible at the time of death, the latent impression (*vāsanā*) produced by prior practice alone is the cause of memory.
"Always" means at all times; "in that" refers to a particular deity and so forth. "Bhāva" means state, cultivation (*bhāvanā*), or latent impression (*vāsanā*). "Tad-bhāvaḥ" means that state.
He by whom that has been cultivated (*bhāvita*)—that is, brought about—is "one whose state of that has been cultivated" (*bhāvita-tad-bhāva*); this is the meaning.
Because *āhitāgni* and others belong to the class of *ākṛti-gaṇa* (formative groups), the word *bhāvita* is placed last in the compound.
Or, it means that his mind has been cultivated—that is, perfumed—by being focused on that [object] through its very nature. //6//
Viśvanātha: Just as it is said, "Remembering Me alone, one attains Me," so too, he says "whomever" (yaṃ yaṃ) to show that by remembering someone other than Me, one attains only that very person.
"Purified" (bhāvitaḥ) means perfumed or made of the same nature [as that object] through its state—that is, through its cultivation or constant contemplation. //6//
Baladeva: It is not a fixed rule that one who remembers Me alone attains My state;
rather, even one who remembers another attains the state of that other. Thus he says, "whichever," meaning whichever object or entity.
One attains that very state immediately after the abandonment of the body of that particular existence;
just as Bharata became a deer at the end of his life because he was thinking of a deer. And the final recollection is of the same object as the prior recollection; thus he says "always" (sadā).
One whose mind is permeated by the memory of that, being cultivated by its very state. //6//
Therefore, at all times remember Me and fight; with mind and intellect offered unto Me, you shall come to Me alone, without doubt. (8.7)

Śrīdhara: Because it is only prior latent impressions (*pūrva-vāsanā*) that serve as the cause for recollection at the time of death, and not because an effort toward recollection is possible for one who is then helpless—therefore [it is said], "Therefore, always remember Me; contemplate Me."
And constant remembrance does not occur without purity of mind;
therefore, "fight, fight"—
the meaning is that you should perform your own duty, such as battle and so forth, for the sake of purifying the mind.
Thus, you by whom the mind—which consists of volition—and the intellect—which consists of resolve—have been offered unto Me, you shall attain Me alone;
of this there is no doubt; there is no uncertainty in this matter. //7//

Madhusūdana: Since, for one who is thus at the mercy of others, it is precisely this final contemplation (*bhāvanā*)—produced by the repeated practice of recollecting [Me] from the past—that is the cause for attaining another body at that time; therefore, for the sake of generating this final contemplation focused on Me, you must first, at all times, recollectedly and with care meditate upon Me as the Lord endowed with attributes (*saguṇa*). If, due to the impurity of your internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), you are unable to recollect Me constantly, then fight for the purification of that internal organ.

For the sake of purifying the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), perform your own duty, such as battle; "yudhya" means "fight. And thus, through the performance of obligatory and occasional duties, when impurity is destroyed and [the mind] is offered unto Me, the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva—

Mind and intellect are characterized by volition and determination; you, who possess these, being thus always intent on meditating upon Me, shall come to Me—shall attain Me alone. Of this there is no doubt; no uncertainty exists in this matter.

And this contemplation of Brahman with attributes (saguṇa-brahma) has been taught for the sake of those who practice meditation (upāsakas), because they depend upon a final meditative realization at the time of death.

However, it should be understood that for those who possess knowledge of Brahman without attributes (nirguṇa-brahma-jñānin), liberation—characterized by the cessation of ignorance—is accomplished simultaneously with the arising of knowledge; therefore, they have no dependence on a final meditative realization. //7//
Viśvanātha: The mind (manas) has the nature of volition (saṅkalpa); the intellect (buddhi) has the nature of determination (vyavasāya). //7//

Baladeva: Since the memory of the past alone is the cause of the final memory, therefore, at all times and at every moment, remember Me and fight; perform your own appropriate duties, such as battle, for the sake of maintaining the world order. Thus, with mind and intellect dedicated to Me, you shall come to Me alone.
But there is nothing else here; let there be no doubt in you regarding this. //7//
With a mind disciplined by the yoga of practice and not wandering elsewhere, O Pārtha, one who meditates upon the supreme divine Person goes to Him. 8.8

Śrīdhara, demonstrating that the practice of constant remembrance is the internal means (*antaraṅga-sādhana*), says: "by the yoga of practice" (*abhyāsa-yogena*). Practice (*abhyāsa*) is a continuous flow of homogeneous mental impressions (*sajātīya-pratyaya-pravāha*);
that itself is the yoga, the means.
By that [mind] which is endowed with that [concentration], one-pointed;
for this very reason, it is a mind whose nature is not to go toward another object.
By that mind.
O Pārtha, by constantly meditating upon the divine, luminous, supreme Person, the Supreme Lord, one goes to Him alone. //8//

Madhusūdana: Thus, having stated the answer to all seven questions, he begins to explain the fruit of recollecting the Lord at the time of departure—characterized by attaining the Lord—in the verse beginning with "abhyāsa" (practice). Practice (*abhyāsa*) is a continuous flow of homogeneous mental impressions (*sajātīya-pratyaya-pravāha*) uninterrupted by heterogeneous impressions (*vijātīya-pratyaya*), as previously explained in the sixth chapter.

That very yoga is *samādhi*; by that [yoga] it is joined—meaning it is occupied with that very [object]. That mind which is empty of mental modifications (*vṛtti*) having the form of the self, by means of that mind, through the proficiency of practice, not going elsewhere—that is, not having the habit of going to another object even without the effort of restraint—by such a mind, one perceives the supreme, unsurpassed, full, divine Person, who shines in heaven (*divi*), within the self that is luminosity (*dyotana*).
"Whoever exists in the sun"— as it is heard in the scripture "and he who is in the sun"—
he goes, that is, he proceeds;
O Pārtha!
Reflecting upon the instruction of the scriptures and the teacher, and meditating upon it. //8//
Viśvanātha: Therefore, for one who practices remembrance, at the time of death, remembrance of Me occurs spontaneously; and by that, one attains Me.

For this reason, He says "the yoga of practice" (*abhyāsa-yoga*), meaning that the yoga of the mind is precisely the remembrance of Me. Practice is the repeated recurrence of the remembrance of Me; [this is] by means of a mind joined with that.

Therefore, by one whose nature it is not to go toward any other object—meaning that through the practice of mindfulness, even mastery over the mind's own nature is achieved—this is the intended sense. //8//
Baladeva: [The Lord] confirms that constant remembrance alone brings about the final remembrance; thus it is said, "by practice.

Practice (*abhyāsa*) is indeed the repetition of remembrance; yoga is that very practice. Therefore, by one who is joined with that and for whom there is no going elsewhere—meaning by one whose mind does not waver toward anything other than that—with a one-pointed mind, contemplating the divine, supreme Person, the glorious Nārāyaṇa Vāsudeva, becoming equal to Him according to the maxim of the worm and the bee.
Being thus, he goes and attains [it]. //8//
He who remembers the Seer, the Ancient, the Ruler, subtler than the subtle— ; BhG 8.9.
The sustainer of all, whose form is inconceivable, whose color is like the sun, beyond the darkness. //9//
Śrīdhara: He further qualifies the Person who is to be meditated upon with two verses, beginning with "the Seer" (kavi).
"The Seer" means the omniscient one, the creator of all branches of knowledge, the ancient one established from time immemorial, and the instructor, that is, the controller.
Subtler than the subtle, exceedingly minute even compared to space, time, and the directions;
the sustainer and nourisher of all;
whose form is inconceivable due to the immeasurability of its majesty; and beyond the reach of the defiled mind and intellect.
"I know this great Puruṣa, resplendent like the sun, beyond darkness"—so says the Śruti. //9//

Madhusūdana—once again, he qualifies that very Person who is to be contemplated and to be reached as "the Seer" (kavi). He is a seer because he possesses transcendent vision; by virtue of seeing all things without exception, such as the past and the future, he is omniscient.
He is ancient (purāṇa), meaning eternal; that is to say, he is without beginning because he is the cause of all.
The instructor, the controller of the entire world;
subtler than the subtle, more minute even than space and other such things, because He is their material cause;
the dispenser of the entire collection of fruits of action to living beings in their various forms, according to the principle: "Therefore, from this [cause], the fruit arises."
One whose immeasurable form cannot be conceived as having the nature of a serpent;
one whose color and radiance illuminate the entire world like the sun—that is to say, the illuminator of the whole universe.
Therefore, he is beyond darkness—beyond the darkness of delusion, characterized by ignorance—meaning that, by virtue of being of the nature of light, he is the adversary of darkness.
"Whoever should remember [Him] and contemplate [Him], he goes to Him"—this is to be connected with what precedes;
or, "he approaches that divine Supreme Person"—this is to be connected with what follows. //9//
Viśvanātha: Without the practice of yoga, it is difficult for the mind to withdraw from the multitude of sense objects;
and it is likewise correct that constant remembrance of the Lord is difficult to achieve without it.
Since devotion is practiced only in conjunction with some form of yogic practice, he describes this "yoga-blended" devotion in five verses beginning with the word *kavi*.

He is the Seer (kavi), the Omniscient One. Even though there are other omniscient beings such as Sanaka and others who exist throughout all time, [the Lord] says "Ancient" (purāṇam) to indicate He is without beginning (anādim). Furthermore, although He is without beginning, He is not merely an inner controller (antaryāmī); He is the Teacher of devotion (bhakty-upadeṣṭā). To show this, He says "Instructor" (anuśāsitāram). This means He is the one who, out of compassion, teaches His own devotees, appearing in forms such as Kṛṣṇa and Rāma.
He says that even such a compassionate one is indeed whose true nature is extremely difficult to discern: "smaller even than the minute.

If so, is he like the individual soul (jīva), merely the size of an atom? To this he replies: "the sustainer of all," meaning that because he supports every single thing and thus pervades everything, he is also of supreme, vast dimension.
This is the sense.
For this very reason, its form is inconceivable.

Although it is of a medium dimension by virtue of having a human-like form, its state of not being illuminated by anything else is expressed by the term "āditya-varṇam," meaning that whose color— its essential nature— is like that of the sun, illuminating both itself and others.
Likewise, the meaning is that although He exists beyond the primordial nature of *tamas* and possesses the power of *māyā*, His essential nature transcends *māyā*. //9//

Baladeva: Since the mind’s exclusive focus on the Lord apart from yoga is difficult to achieve, he describes devotion conjoined with yoga through five verses beginning with "the sage" (*kavim*). "The sage" means the omniscient one;
"the instructor" means the one who teaches for one's welfare by appearing in forms such as Raghunātha.
It is established that [the Self] enters within even the subtle atom (*aṇu*), for it is subtler than the subtle;
and thus the Śruti says: "He has entered within as the ruler of people.
Furthermore, it declares its pervasiveness despite being subtler than the subtle, by saying "of all."
[He is] the creator and sustainer of the entire world.

Now, how is this consistent? To that he says: His form is inconceivable, his essential nature is beyond thought; for it is said that Brahman alone, though of the form of the Person (*puruṣa-vidha*), is of intermediate dimension, yet subtler than the subtlest.
Since it is stated that the creator of all things possesses the dimension of an atom,
and also possesses the dimension of the supreme great,
there is no room here for logical reasoning.
He states its self-luminosity and luminosity of others with the word "āditya" (like the sun); the meaning is that it illuminates both itself and others like the sun.
He states its lack of contact with even the scent of *māyā* with the word "tamasaḥ" (beyond darkness);
it stands beyond *māyā*, which is darkness.
The meaning is that he is beyond illusion (māyā), even though he possesses the power of illusion (māyin).
The connection with the following verse is: "He who remembers such a Person at every moment attains that Supreme Person. //9//
At the time of departure, with a steady mind, endowed with devotion and indeed by the power of yoga;
Having properly fixed his vital breath between the eyebrows, he attains that supreme, divine Person. //10//
Śrīdhara: "At the time of departure" means:

having pierced through the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) along with its phenomenal expansion (*saprapañca*), he who abides—such a person, one who at the time of death should remember with a mind endowed with devotion, steady and free from distraction.
The cause for the immobility of the mind is this:

by the power of yoga, having properly caused the vital breath (prāṇa) to enter the space between the eyebrows through the path of the suṣumṇā, he attains that Supreme Person, whose nature is the Supreme Self, divine and luminous. //10//

Madhusūdana: When does an excess [of devotion] arise in the remembrance of Him? To this he says, "At the time of departure" (prayāṇa). At the time of departure—that is, at the time of death—one should remember that Person with a steady and one-pointed mind; this is understood from the context. Of what nature is he? He is endowed with devotion (*bhakti*), which consists of supreme love directed toward the Supreme Lord.

He is endowed with the power of yoga— that is, the power of *samādhi*— and with the collection of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced thereby, which are opposed to the latent impressions of the state of emergence (*vyutthāna*).
Having thus first brought [the mind] under control within the heart-lotus, he then, by means of the upward-moving *suṣumnā* channel according to the path taught by the Guru,
having entered and fixed the vital breath (*prāṇa*) in the *ājñā-cakra* between the eyebrows through the sequence of conquering the stages (*bhūmi*), remains perfectly vigilant.

Having ascended from the aperture of Brahmā (*brahma-randhra*), that very practitioner of meditation approaches—that is, attains—the Supreme Person, who is characterized by being the ancient Seer (*kavi*), the Instructor, and so forth, and who is divine, consisting of light. //10//
Viśvanātha: At the time of departure—that is, at the time of death—one who is endowed with that devotion consisting of constant remembrance by means of a mind that is *acala*, meaning motionless;
how is there such motionlessness of the mind?
To this he says: "by the power of yoga," that is, by the power of the practice of yoga.
He shows the method of yoga [as follows]: in the center of the two eyebrows, at the ājñā-cakra. //10//

Baladeva: That person who, endowed with devotion, love for the Supreme Self, the power of yoga, and the accumulation of impressions born of meditative absorption (samādhi), should at the time of departure—the moment of death—commemorate that Puruṣa with an unshakable and one-pointed mind;
[the Lord] describes the method of yoga, beginning with "between the eyebrows."
Having caused the vital breath to enter and firmly establish it in the *ājñā*-cakra between the eyebrows, being perfectly attentive, he approaches that Puruṣa. //10//
That imperishable which those who know the Vedas declare, and which the ascetics, free from passion, enter;
I shall declare to you in brief that goal for which those desiring it practice the life of celibacy (brahmacarya). //11//
Śrīdhara: Desiring to prescribe the practice of the *praṇava* as an internal means even beyond mere practice [of other methods], he makes this declaration: "That which is imperishable.
This refers to that imperishable which those who know the meaning of the Vedas declare;
for the Śruti says: "Under the governance of this very Imperishable, O Gārgī, the sun and moon stand held apart."
Those from whom passion has departed are "free from passion" (*vīta-rāga*).
Those who enter that [state] are the "strivers" (*yatayaḥ*), those who are diligent;
and desiring to know that, they practice the life of a religious student (*brahmacarya*) in the teacher's household.
That state (*pada*) is what is reached or attained; thus, *pada* means that which is to be attained.
I shall declare it "in brief," that is, in summary;
the meaning is that I shall explain the means for attaining that. //11//

Madhusūdana: Now, when the recollection of the Blessed One at the time of meditation is required by whatever name [is used]—[it is said]: "That state which all the Vedas declare, and which all austerities proclaim..."
"Desiring which they lead the life of celibacy (brahmacarya), that goal I declare to you in brief: it is 'Om'.

Because this is established by such scriptural passages as these, he begins with the words "That Imperishable," in order to restrict that remembrance to the syllable *praṇava* alone, and not to other mantras or the like.

That which the knowers of the Veda call the imperishable syllable known as Oṃ is indeed that Imperishable, O Gārgī; by such statements as "neither gross nor subtle, neither short nor long," the Brahmins establish it through the negation of all specific attributes. Though it is realized only by those skilled in the means of valid knowledge, they have nonetheless experienced it as the goal to be reached by the liberated; thus he says: "they enter."

Through right vision (*samyag-darśana*) regarding its true nature (*svarūpa*), that Imperishable (*akṣara*) which ascetics—those disciplined in effort, renunciants free from passion and devoid of desire—seek;
not only has it been experienced by the perfected ones (*siddhas*), but even for practitioners (*sādhakas*), every exertion is for its sake. Thus he says:
desiring to know it, lifelong celibates (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacārins*) practice their celibacy through austerities such as dwelling in the teacher’s family (*gurukula*).
I shall explain—that state called the Imperishable (akṣara), which is to be attained—to you in brief, that is, in summary, so that understanding may arise for you.
The intention is: "Therefore, do not be distressed, wondering how that Imperishable is to be known by me."

And here too, by such statements as, "Furthermore, he who meditates upon the Supreme Person with this very syllable 'Om' consisting of three measures, he attains Him," meditation— which has gradual liberation as its fruit for those of dull and middling intellects, being performed either as a denoter of the Supreme Brahman or as a symbol (pratīka) like an image— is indeed taught in this context as well.

This was intended by the Blessed One. Therefore, from this point until the end of the chapter, Viśvanātha explains the following range of topics: the worship of the syllable *oṃ* accompanied by *yoga* and *dhāraṇā*, its fruit, one's own true nature (*svarūpa*), non-return from that state, and the path thereto. [Objection: But surely, by the mere statement "having fixed the vital breath (*prāṇa*) between the eyebrows," *yoga* is not fully understood.
Therefore, in that yoga, what is the method, what is to be recited, or what is to be meditated upon?
In response to the expectation, "Please tell me briefly what is to be attained," he says with three verses beginning with "That which":

"That very syllable *om*, which is the Brahman denoted by the single syllable, into which ascetics enter—that is the *pada* (the goal), so called because it is reached (*padyate*) or gone to; it is that which is to be attained.
It is the *saṅgraha* (compendium) because it is thoroughly grasped by means of this; I shall explain it along with its means (*upāya*). Listen. (11)
Baladeva: Now, one might object that by merely directing the vital breath (prāṇa) between the eyebrows, yoga is not fully understood;
therefore, in response to the expectation—"Tell me its method, the mantra to be recited there, and the goal to be attained"—he speaks in three verses beginning with "That syllable" (yad akṣaram).
They declare that the one Brahman alone is the imperishable (akṣara), the signifier "Om."

The ascetics, free from passion and with ignorance destroyed, enter—that is, they attain—that Brahman which is the object of expression, whose sole essence is pure consciousness. Desiring to know that Brahman which possesses both forms, lifelong students practice celibacy characterized by residence in the teacher’s house and so forth. I shall explain that state, together with its summary means, so that you may attain that knowledge without effort.
According to its etymological derivation (*nirukti*), it is called *saṃgraha* because reality (*tattva*) is correctly grasped by means of it; thus, it is the method of compendium (*upāya*). //11//

Having restrained all the gates [of the senses] and having confined the mind within the heart, placing the vital breath (prāṇa) in the head, he remains established in the practice of yogic concentration (yoga-dhāraṇā). (8.12)
Uttering the single-syllable Brahman "Om" and remembering Me, he who departs, casting off the body, goes to the supreme goal. 13.
Śrīdhara: With two verses beginning with "sarvāṇi," he states the means along with its constituent parts as previously promised.
"Having restrained all the doors of the senses" means having withdrawn them;
that is, not perceiving external objects through the eyes and other sense organs.
Having restrained the mind within the heart— meaning, not recollecting external objects—
and having fixed the vital breath (prāṇa) between the eyebrows at the crown of the head, he remained established in the steadiness of yoga, having resorted to its concentration (dhāraṇā). //12//

"Om. The single syllable "Om" is indeed Brahman, either because it denotes Brahman or because it is a symbol (*pratīka*) of Brahman, like an image. One who departs the body while uttering—that is, pronouncing—it and simultaneously remembering Me, who am denoted by it, and goes forth with excellence by way of the path of light (*arcir-ādi-mārga*), attains—that is, reaches—the supreme, most excellent goal, which is My own state. //13//
Madhusūdana: Regarding that which was promised as "I shall explain," he states the subject matter along with its prerequisites in two verses, beginning with "All doors.

Having restrained all the doors of the senses—that is, having withdrawn them from their respective objects—he does not perform the grasping of objects such as sound through the ears and other senses, which have been rendered averse to them through the practice of perceiving the defects in sense-objects.
One might think that even when the external senses are restrained, the mind might still continue its activity; therefore, he says: "and having restrained the mind in the heart.

By means of practice and dispassion—both of which were explained in the sixth chapter—one restrains the mind in the region of the heart and brings it to a state of cessation (nirvṛttikatā); the meaning is that one does not engage in even internal reflection upon objects.
Thus, having completely restrained all the external and internal doors of perception, and having fully suppressed even the vital breath— the door of action— from all sides, one should,

through the sequence of conquering the elements, place it at the crown of the head; then, by the path taught by the Guru, one should cause it to enter between the eyebrows and above that, performing the yogic concentration (*dhāraṇā*) upon the Self, which takes the form of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) focused on the Self.
"Established in the self" means for the sake of the divine function of the deity. //12//
"Om"—this single syllable, because it denotes Brahman or because it is a symbol (pratīka) for Brahman as embodied in the image, while uttering or pronouncing "Brahman";
by the mere statement "uttering 'Om'," the purpose is served, and the phrase "the single syllable" is added for the sake of praise, describing it as being effortless to pronounce.
Alternatively, it means: while uttering "Om," one should remember me—the single syllable, the one without a second, the imperishable, all-pervading Brahman—whose meaning is "Om."

Chanting the *praṇava* and meditating upon Me, who am its designated referent, he who departs from the body through the channel at the crown of the head travels by way of the path of the gods (*devayāna*); having gone to the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*), at the conclusion of those enjoyments, he attains the supreme, most excellent goal, which is My own form.
In this regard, Patañjali, having stated that "for those with intense ardor, the attainment of samādhi is near" (YS 1.21), further stated, "or from devotion to Īśvara" (1.23).
And devotion has been explained as: "the designator of Him is the syllable Om" (1.27).
"Repetition of that [mantra] and meditation on its meaning" (1.28),
and "The perfection of samādhi results from devotion to the Lord" (2.45).
However, here it is stated that the attainment of the supreme goal occurs directly from that [devotion].

Therefore, it should be explained that while uttering the single-syllable Brahman "Aum," which signifies non-contradiction (*avirodha*), he remained established in the yogic concentration (*yoga-dhāraṇā*) upon Me;
or else, because it is logical that [the syllable] yields various fruits, it is not something to be suppressed. //13//

Viśvanātha: Stating the aforementioned meaning, he describes the method for yoga: having restrained all the gateways of the senses, such as the eyes, by withdrawing them from external objects; having confined the mind within the heart itself and not forming conceptualizations regarding other objects;

and having fixed the vital breath (prāṇa) between the eyebrows at the crown of the head—one should practice the concentration of yoga (*yoga-dhāraṇā*), which consists of the contemplation of my form from the tips of the nails to the crest of the hair.

Taking refuge [in Me], uttering and pronouncing the single syllable "Om," which is the very nature of Brahman, and while meditating upon and recollecting Me who am signified by that syllable, he attains the supreme goal, which is My same world (sālokya). //12-13//
Baladeva says: He describes the method of yoga with the words "all," etc.

Having restrained all external doors of perception, such as the ears and so forth, and having withdrawn them from objects such as sound by means of the practice of perceiving their defects, one should direct the mind toward the restraint of the ears and other senses while they are still apprehending those objects through that very process of turning away from them.
Therefore, he says: "With me situated in the heart, having restrained the mind—the door to internal knowledge—and having fixed it there while remembering them even with the mind;

then, having first placed the vital breath (prāṇa)—the door of action—upon the crown of the head, having mastered it within the heart-lotus, [one proceeds] by the upward path of the suṣumṇā according to the method taught by the Guru, through the sequence of conquering the stages (bhūmis), to the space between the eyebrows, above that, and finally to the aperture of Brahman (brahma-randhra)."
And having established himself in my yogic concentration (yoga-dhāraṇā), remaining fixed in meditation upon me from head to toe,

uttering the expressive Brahman "Om" within— that is, pronouncing it internally— he praises that [Brahman] as the "single syllable," meaning that it is both one and primary, and that syllable is imperishable; thus, while recollecting me, the Supreme Self, who am signified by that [syllable].
He who departs while casting off the body in this state of meditation attains the supreme goal: residence in my own world. //12-13//
For that yogi who is constantly disciplined and who remembers Me daily with an undivided mind, I am easily attained, O Pārtha. (8.14)

Śrīdhara: And thus, at the time of death, the attainment of Me through dhāraṇā occurs only for one who possesses constant practice, not for anyone else; this is what he recalls from what was previously stated by the word "ananya. One whose mind (cetas) is not directed toward anything else is "ananya."
Being thus situated,
for him who remembers me constantly, without interruption, eternally, and day by day—
for that person who is ever-disciplined and composed, I am attainable with ease, and not for anyone else. //14//

Madhusūdana: Regarding one who, due to the impairment caused by the obstruction of the vital breath (vāyu), is unable to leave the body at will by entering the life-force (prāṇa) through the channel leading to the crown of the head, but instead leaves the body helplessly only upon the exhaustion of karma—what becomes of him? To this he says: "With mind fixed on no other" (ananya-cetāḥ).

He whose mind finds no object other than Me is "one whose mind is fixed on no other" (*ananya-cetas*); for such a yogi who remembers Me constantly, without interruption, and perpetually throughout his entire life— whether he casts off his body while under his own control or otherwise— I, the Supreme Lord, am easily attained with ease by him who is ever-disciplined and whose mind is perpetually concentrated, whereas this is not so for others.
The intended meaning is: "O Pārtha, although I am exceedingly difficult to attain, I am very easy for you to reach; do not fear.

Here, the genitive case in *tasya* (*of him*) is used in the sense of a general relationship (*sambandha-sāmānya*), because [the use of the genitive] with the agent (*kartṛ*) is prohibited by rules such as *na lokāvyaya-niṣṭhā-khal-artha-tṛṇām*.
And here, by the phrase "with undistracted mind," "reverence" is meant as extreme respect;
by "constantly" (*satatam*), uninterruptedness is expressed, and by "always" (*nityaśas*), the long duration of the recollection is stated.
Therefore, that [recollection], when practiced with long duration, uninterruptedness, and reverence, becomes firmly established (YS 1.14).
Thus, the doctrine of Patañjali is followed here.
In that context, although "it" (saḥ) refers to practice (*abhyāsa*), it culminates in remembrance (*smaraṇa*).

Therefore, until the end of one's life, constant contemplation of the Blessed One, free from any other distraction at every moment, is the cause for the supreme goal; however, the voluntary departure of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) through the cranial channel (*mūrdhanī nāḍī*)—
Let it be so, or let it not; there is no excessive insistence on this point. //14//

Viśvanātha: Thus, having described devotion as the primary subject along with its ancillaries— first as mixed with *karma* by the verse beginning with "ārtaḥ," then again as mixed with *karma* by the phrase "for liberation from old age and death," and as mixed with *yoga* by the verses beginning with "the ancient Seer"— he now speaks of the supreme, attributeless (*nirguṇa*), and exclusive (*kevala*) devotion with the words "ananya-cetāḥ" (one whose mind is focused on no other).

He is one whose mind does not find anything else to be practiced as a duty— whether it be another action or the yoga of knowledge— nor any other deity to be worshipped, nor even heaven, liberation, and so forth, as something to be attained.

He who remembers me constantly and always—without regard for time, place, recipient, purity, and so forth, but rather eternally and indeed every single day—for that devotee, I am easily attained; I am obtained with ease.
The sense is that this is because there is no admixture of the hardships associated with the practice of yoga, knowledge, and the like.

For one who is constantly disciplined and always desires my yoga, the suffix -kta is used in the sense of the future according to the rule *āśaṃsāyāṃ bhūtavac ca*; thus, it refers to the yoga that is hoped for in the future.
"Of the yogin" means of one possessed of the yoga of devotion (*bhakti-yoga*), or alternatively, of one whose connection to yoga consists of service (*dāsya*), friendship (*sakhya*), and so forth.
[The result accrues] to one who possesses that [merit]. //14//

Baladeva: Having thus taught devotion mixed with yoga for those who desire liberation alone, He now teaches pure devotion—called "exclusive devotion" (ekabhakti)—for His own knowers who desire Him alone, beginning with the words "ananya... (unswerving). That person whose mind is "ananya-cetas"—meaning whose mind is not directed toward any means other than Me, such as karma-yoga and the like, nor toward any goal other than Me, such as heaven or liberation; [he is one who worships Me].
Or, he whose mind is constantly and at all times— without regard for purity of place, time, and so forth—

always and daily remembers me, the Lord of All who appeared in many forms such as Yaśodā’s suckling child, Nṛsiṃha, and Raghunātha; and who contemplates me during worship, recitation, and other rites— I, knowing his love, [am pleased].
It is "easily attainable" (sulabha), meaning it is obtained with ease because it is free from contact with the hardships of performing rituals, practicing yoga, and so forth.
The word "tasya" (of that) uses the genitive case in the sense of a general relationship, for its use in the sense of the agent is prohibited by the rule "na lokāvyayaniṣṭhākhalarthatṛnām."
Being unable to endure separation from such a one, I myself reveal that Self to him, bringing to maturity the means for its attainment and removing all that is adverse to it.
And the Śruti says thus: "He is to be obtained by whomsoever He chooses; to him this Self reveals His own form."
And He Himself will say: "I give that yoga of wisdom by which they come unto Me," and so forth.

To the question "Of what kind [of person]? He says: "Of one who is ever... (nitya-). This refers to one who always desires union with Me. According to the rule *āśaṃsāyāṃ bhūtavac ca* ("the past participle suffix is used for the future when there is a sense of expectation"), the suffix *-kta* is applied even to the future union that is being hoped for.
Yogins who possess relationships such as servitude or friendship toward Me. //14//
Having come to Me, the high-souled ones, having attained the supreme perfection, do not undergo rebirth, which is transient and an abode of suffering. (8.15)
Śrīdhara: If you are thus easily accessible, what of it?
To this he says, "Me.
Great-souled ones possessing the characteristics described above, being My devotees, having attained Me, do not undergo birth again, which is the locus of suffering and characterized by death.
Because they have attained the supreme, perfect accomplishment which is indeed liberation;
or rather, having come to Me, they do not again encounter the foundation—the locus—of the sufferings of rebirth. //15//
Madhusūdana: Regarding the doubt as to whether those who have attained the Blessed One return again or not, He says "mām" (Me) to show that they do not return.

Having attained Me, the Lord, they do not obtain birth again—that is, the connection with a human or other body—which is a repository of suffering, a place of manifold miseries such as dwelling in the womb and emerging through the passage of the birth canal; it is impermanent, unstable, and for all practical purposes vanished as soon as seen. The meaning is that they do not return.

Since those great souls—whose internal organs are free from the impurities of *rajas* and *tamas*, who possess pure *sattva*, and in whom right vision has arisen—have attained supreme, most excellent perfection, that is, liberation, at the end of their worldly enjoyments;
by saying here, "Having reached Me, they have attained perfection," the gradual liberation of the devotees is shown. //15//

Viśvanātha: To the question of what would happen to one who has attained you, he says "mām" (me). They do not obtain a birth that is a repository of suffering—full of misery—and impermanent; rather, they obtain a birth full of happiness, equal to my own birth.
"Śāśvata, dhruva, nitya, sadānana, and sanātana" are synonyms for "eternal," according to the *Amara-kośa*.

The underlying meaning is this: when my birth occurs in the house of Vasudeva—filled with bliss, eternal, and non-material—it is at that very time that the birth of those devotees of mine who are ever-attached to me also takes place, and not at any other time.
"Others," meaning other devotees, attain "supreme perfection"; however, those whose minds are focused on no other [attain] "supreme perfection," which means becoming attendants in My pastimes.
By this, the superiority of the visible [devotees] is illuminated over all other devotees characterized as previously described. //15//
Baladeva: In response to the inquiry as to what fruit would accrue to one who has attained Her, He says "mām" (Me).
Having approached—that is, having reached—Me, whose characteristics have been described, they do not obtain birth again in the phenomenal world; the meaning is that they do not return.
As to what kind of birth [they avoid], He says: it is an abode of suffering, filled with many afflictions such as dwelling in the womb and so forth.
"Non-eternal" means impermanent, characterized by being seen and then destroyed; "eternal," however, means stable and permanent—thus says Amara.

Since they have attained me alone as their supreme, most excellent *saṃsiddhi* (perfection) and *gati* (goal)—for he will later say, "The Unmanifest is called the Imperishable; they call that the supreme goal"—what kind of people are those great-souled ones? They are those of exceedingly noble minds, [who have approached] the treasure-house of consciousness and bliss who is intent upon favoring his devotees.
Disregarding all else, such as the attainment of equality with Me (sārṣṭi), they consider me alone to be their very life-breath, for my entire being is dependent upon my devotees;
therefore, they have attained perfection through me alone.
Herein lies the superiority of this person of undivided mind and exclusive devotion over those who are devoted to me but are established in themselves.
It is said: //15//
"O Arjuna, all worlds, up to the realm of Brahmā, are subject to return; but having attained Me, O son of Kuntī, there is no rebirth. (8.16)
Śrīdhara: All living beings, even those who have performed great meritorious deeds, are born [again];
however, My devotees are not born like them—this he states with the words "ā-brahma" (up to Brahmā).
This means pervading up to Brahmā’s world, the Satyaloka. //16//

Madhusūdana: Since it has been stated that those who have attained the Blessed One and possess right vision do not return, it follows as a matter of course that those who turn away from Him and lack right vision must return;
thus [the Lord] says, "From the world of Brahmā" (*ābrahma*). A "world" (*bhuvana*) is so called because beings (*bhūtāni*) come into existence (*bhavanti*) therein. It refers to the realm.
The prefix *ā-* is used here in the sense of inclusion (*abhividhi*).

Together with the world of Brahmā, all worlds whatsoever are the enjoyments for those who are averse to Me and lack right vision; they are characterized by returning, meaning they have the nature of recurring.
In the reading *brahma-bhavanāt*, the word *bhavana* means a place of residence; thus, the meaning remains the same.
"O Arjuna, O Great Being who is self-evidently established! Is there, for those who have reached you in that same manner, a return once more? No," he says: "But having approached Me alone, the Lord.
The word "but" (*tu*) is intended to highlight the distinction from other worlds, or it serves as an emphatic particle (*avadhāraṇa*).
"O Kaunteya, for those who have attained Me alone, there is no rebirth; that is to say, there is no return.

Here, O Arjuna, by the two forms of address—Kaunteya and Arjuna—the purity of both one's essential nature (*svarūpa*) and one's causal conditions (*kāraṇa*) is indicated for the sake of attaining perfect knowledge. In this regard, the following systematic arrangement applies:

For those who have reached the world of Brahman through meditations that yield liberation by stages (*krama-mukti*), and who have attained right vision (*samyag-darśana*) while there, there is liberation together with Brahman.

However, for those who have gone there by means of the knowledge of the five fires (*pañcāgni-vidyā*) and the like—even though they do not have that as their specific resolve (*atat-kratu*)—rebirth is inevitable. Therefore, it is said with reference to liberation by stages: "He attains the world of Brahman and does not return again."
"Non-return [is established] by the word"—this is the justification found in both the Śruti and the Sūtra.

Regarding the other [paths], there is no return here; for the specific qualifications "to this" and "to this human whirlpool" (imam mānavam āvartam) indicate that there is a return elsewhere, specifically from the kalpa during which the journey occurs.
Viśvanātha explains: "All living beings, even those of great merit, are born again; but My devotees, however, are not born again," as expressed in the verse beginning with "up to Brahmā."
The world of Brahmā is the Satyaloka; having pervaded that [world]. //16//

Baladeva says: "But those who are averse to Me, even if they attain worlds such as heaven through specific types of ritual action (*karma*), fall from them. He states this with the words beginning "up to Brahmā" (*ābrahma*).
The particle *ā* here denotes inclusion (*abhividhi*), meaning that the world of Brahmā (*brahma-bhuvana*) is encompassed.

Together with the world of Brahmā, all the worlds beginning with heaven, as well as the individual souls (*jīvas*) residing therein, upon the exhaustion of their respective karmas, are subject to return; they obtain rebirth on earth once again.
The repetition of the phrase "having come to Me" (*mām upetya*) is for the purpose of providing firm reinforcement.

Here, this should be understood: those who have gone to the world of Brahmā (*brahma-loka*) by means of the knowledge of the five fires (*pañcāgni-vidyā*), by dying in a great battle, and so forth, shall fall when their enjoyment there ends.

However, those who are devoted to the Supreme Lord with steadfastness (*sa-niṣṭhāḥ*), having gone there while experiencing the worlds of heaven and so forth in succession, do not fall from that state.

But at the destruction of that world, there is the attainment of the world of the Supreme Lord together with its Ruler: "When the universal dissolution has arrived, all those who have perfected themselves enter the supreme state at the end of the highest [Brahmā]."
Because of this traditional teaching (smaraṇa). //16//
Those people who know that the day of Brahmā extends for a thousand yugas and that his night likewise ends after a thousand yugas are truly knowers of day and night. (8.17)

Śrīdhara: But surely, by such statements from the Purāṇas as, "Ascetics who are charitable, free from passion, and patient attain a station above the three worlds, which is devoid of worldly beings," it is understood that Maharloka and the other realms are superior to the [lower] three worlds.

Anticipating the objection, "If all things are subject to destruction, how can there be such a distinction [between them]? and intending to show that this distinction is caused by their duration being long or short— demonstrating that according to his own measure, the three worlds arise day after day during the life of Brahmā, who lives for a hundred years, and undergo dissolution night after night— he states the measure of Brahmā’s day and night with the words beginning "sahasra."

Those who know that day of Brahmā, whose limit and conclusion is a thousand *yugas*, and those who, by the power of yoga, know that night which has a thousand *yugas* as its end— they alone are omniscient people who truly know day and night. However, those whose knowledge consists merely of the movement of the moon and the sun do not truly know day and night.
Because their vision is limited.
Here, by the word "yuga," the four-yuga cycle is intended; for it is stated in the *Viṣṇu Purāṇa* that "a thousand four-yuga cycles is said to be a day of Brahmā.
Furthermore, the mention of "Brahmā" is intended as an illustration for those inhabitants of Maharloka and the other higher worlds.
In this regard, the method for calculating time is as follows:
that which is one year for humans is a single day and night for the gods.
By means of such days and nights, through the reckoning of fortnights, months, and so forth, twelve thousand years constitute a *catur-yuga*.
A thousand cycles of the four yugas constitute one day of Brahmā; his night is of the same duration.
By such days and nights, proceeding through the sequence of fortnights, months, and so forth, a hundred years is the supreme lifespan of Brahmā. //17//
Madhusūdana says: "All worlds, including the world of Brahmā, are subject to return.

Why? Because they are limited by time. He explains this with the word "sahasra": measured by human reckoning, that which has a limit or end consisting of a thousand yugas—that is, a thousand cycles of the four ages—is what is meant.
"A thousand cycles of four yugas is said to be a day of Brahmā"—such is the statement of the Purāṇas.

Those who know such a day of Brahmā, the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati), and likewise know his night, which ends after a thousand cycles of four yugas—that is, reaching the limit of a thousand sets of four yugas—they are the "knowers of day and night"; they alone are the yogis who truly understand day and night.

However, those who understand [the day and night] solely by means of the motion of the moon and sun do not truly know the day and night; the intention is that this is because their vision is very limited. //17//
