Viśvanātha: [Objection] But surely, according to the statement in the Second Canto, "Immortality, security, and fearlessness were placed upon the heads of the Three-headed One" (BhP 2.6.19), since the fearlessness of the world of Brahmā is heard of in the opinion of some, and because it is even desired by renunciants, is it not possible that there is no falling for those residing there? [Reply] Not so.
Suggesting that even Brahmā, the lord of that world, would suffer a fall, let alone others, he says "sahasra":

that day of Brahmā, whose limit or conclusion consists of a thousand *yugas*, is known by those people who are experts in the scriptures; those people who know the day and night are aware that his night also ends with a thousand *yugas*.
By such days and nights, proceeding through the sequence of fortnights, months, and years, the supreme lifespan of Brahmā is one hundred years.
At the end of this period, his fall occurs; however, it is indicated that for no devotee of Viṣṇu does there exist even such liberation as that of Brahmā. //17//
Baladeva: With the intention that all worlds, beginning with heaven and ending with Satyaloka, perish because they are limited by time, he says "sahasra" (thousand).

That which they know as the day of the four-faced Brahmā is the limit of a thousand yugas according to human calculation; for there is a Smṛti text stating, "A thousand cycles of the four yugas is called a day of Brahmā.
Thus, it is that whose end or conclusion consists of a thousand four-yuga periods.

Only those people who are practitioners of yoga (yogins) and knowers of day and night understand that his night ends at the conclusion of four thousand yugas; others are not knowers of day and night. This is an illustration for those residing in Maharloka and the other higher worlds. The meaning is this: one human year is a day and night for the gods; by calculating with such days and nights, [one arrives at] fortnights, months, and so forth.

Twelve thousand years constitute a *catur-yuga*; a thousand such *catur-yugas* form a day of Brahmā, and his night is of equal duration. By calculating months and so forth with such days and nights, his lifespan is one hundred years. At the end of that period, there is the destruction of that world and of those who dwell within it.
Repetition is established. //17//
At the arrival of day, all manifest beings emerge from the unmanifest; at the arrival of night, they dissolve back into that very same state known as the unmanifest. (8.18)
Śrīdhara: What follows from that? To this he says, "from the unmanifest" (avyaktāt).
The unmanifest form of the effect is of the nature of its cause.
Therefore, from that unmanifest cause-form, the manifest entities— the moving and non-moving beings— appear;
they emerge when day arrives, at the beginning of Brahmā’s day,
and likewise when night arrives, during Brahmā’s sleep.
They go to dissolution in that very cause which is designated as the Unmanifest (avyakta).
Alternatively, the phrase "those who know day and night" is not being prescribed here;
rather, those well-known people who know day and night [understand that] at the arrival of that day which they know to belong to Brahmā, the manifest entities emerge from the Unmanifest.
And the connection between the two [phrases] is as follows: "on the arrival of that night which they know, they dissolve. //18//

Madhusūdana: By the aforementioned days and nights, calculated by the sequence of fortnights and months, the full lifespan of Prajāpati is one hundred years; thus, being limited by time, he is impermanent.
Therefore, from that world, there is necessarily a return.

As for those who are inferior to him, since their [lives] are limited to a mere day, what need is there to say that they must return from their respective worlds? Thus he says: "From the unmanifest... (avyaktāt).

Since it is only the daily creation and dissolution that have been introduced as the subject here, and since space and the other elements exist therein, the state of non-manifestation (*avyakta*) is not being described by the term "unmanifest";
rather, it refers specifically to the state of Prajāpati’s sleep—
that is to say, Prajāpati in his state of sleep.

At the arrival of the day, during the time of Prajāpati’s awakening, from the unmanifest—which is the state of his sleep—manifestations consisting of bodies, objects, and so forth, which constitute the enjoyments of experience, come forth; that is, they become manifest through their capacity for worldly activity.

At the arrival of the night, at the time of his sleep, all those aforementioned manifestations dissolve and disappear back into that very same thing called the unmanifest, from which they had emerged.
When the previously mentioned cause, Prajāpati, is in the state of sleep. //18//
Viśvanātha: As for those who are more recent than that and reside within the three worlds, their dissolution occurs day after day; thus he says, "from the unmanifest" (*avyaktāt*).

Regarding this, the venerable Madhusūdana Sarasvatī states that because space and the other elements exist during both the daily creation and dissolution, the term "unmanifest" refers specifically to Prajāpati in his state of sleep.

Consequently, from the "unmanifest"—that is, from Prajāpati in his state of sleep—manifestations in the form of bodies, objects, and so forth, which are the grounds of experience and capable of worldly transaction, come into being.
At the arrival of night, at the time of his sleep, they dissolve and disappear into him alone. //18//
Baladeva: But for those who exist within the three worlds and are posterior to Him, their destruction occurs at the end of Brahmā’s day; thus he says, "From the Unmanifest.

At the arrival of the day, during the time of Brahmā’s waking, all manifested entities—consisting of bodies, senses, objects of enjoyment, and places of enjoyment—proceed forth, that is, they arise from that Unmanifest state which is His sleep.
At the arrival of night, during His time of sleep, they dissolve—that is, they become unmanifest—in that very cause known as the Unmanifest, which is the state of sleep belonging to Brahmā.
In this context, the term "unmanifest" (avyakta) does not denote the Pradhāna, because the passage begins with the description of the daily creation and dissolution;
furthermore, at that time, the ether and other elements already exist.
Rather, its meaning is Brahman itself in the state of deep sleep. //18//
This same multitude of beings, having come into existence again and again, dissolves helplessly at the arrival of night; it comes forth again at the arrival of day, O Pārtha. (8.19)

Śrīdhara: And here, warding off the suspicion that what has been done would perish or that what has not been done would accrue [to one], he shows the uninterrupted flow of the succession of creation and dissolution for the sake of dispassion, saying "the multitude of beings" (bhūta-grāma).
"Beings" (bhūtānām) refers to moving and non-moving living creatures;
"multitude" (grāmaḥ) means a collection.

He who existed previously is this very same one; having come into being again and again at the arrival of day, he dissolves again and again at the arrival of night. Having dissolved repeatedly, he comes forth once more at the arrival of day, being powerless and dependent upon karma and other factors—this is the meaning of "none other. //19//

Madhusūdana: Even though [the self] is thus subject to rapid destruction, there is no cessation for one situated in *saṃsāra*, because of the repeated manifestation [of the self] through the power of afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and so forth, over which one has no control; and because once manifested, it again undergoes disappearance solely by the power of those very afflictions and the like. For all living beings revolving in *saṃsāra* lack independence, and being thus powerless, they remain bound to the continuous succession of sufferings such as birth and death.

He says "the multitude of beings" (*bhūta-grāma*) for the purpose of generating dispassion—[thinking] "enough with this saṃsāra"—and to avoid the fallacies of the destruction of what has been done (*kṛta-nāśa*) and the acquisition of what has not been done (*akṛtābhyāgama*), because [beings] appear again and again with identical names and forms.

The "multitude of beings" is a collection of beings characterized as both stationary and moving; that very same [multitude] which existed in the previous kalpa is born again in this kalpa, and it is not something else in every kalpa.
And furthermore:
because he does not accept the doctrine that the effect is non-existent [prior to its production], [the text says]:
"The Creator fashioned the sun and the moon just as before."
Heaven and earth, the intermediate space, and likewise the celestial realm.
Thus says the Śruti (Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad 1.65):
"Because names and forms are the same, there is no contradiction even in the case of recurrence, as seen from both scripture and tradition" (Vedāntasūtra 1.3.30).
And because of this principle:
"helpless" means dependent on ignorance, desire, karma, and so forth.
O Pārtha, the rest is clear. 19.
Viśvanātha: In this very way, the "group" (grāma) of beings refers to the multitude of living creatures, both moving and unmoving. //19//

Baladeva: Lest there arise the suspicion that there is a loss of what was done (*kṛta-hāni*) or the acquisition of what was not done (*akṛtābhyāgama*)—namely, that those who have dissolved [into the source] will not be born again—he says "the aggregate of beings" (*bhūta*) to dispel that.

The "aggregate of beings" (*bhūta-grāmaḥ*), meaning the multitude of stable and moving living creatures, being "unfree" (*avaśaḥ*), that is, dependent on karma, [is thus reborn]. It is therefore stated that for the discerning, detachment (*vairāgya*) is appropriate toward this phenomenal world (*prapañca*) which is crowded with such a continuous flow of birth and death. //19//
But beyond that unmanifested state, there is another unmanifested being, eternal; it does not perish even when all beings perish. (8.20)

Śrīdhara: Having elaborated upon the impermanence of the worlds, he now elaborates upon the permanence of the nature of the Supreme Lord with two verses beginning with "para. That eternal (*sanātana*), beginningless (*anādi*) Being, who is distinct from and different in character than that unmanifest (*avyakta*) which is the cause of the moving and the unmoving, and who is beyond even that [unmanifest] as its cause—being invisible to the eyes and other senses—he does not perish even when all beings characterized as effects and causes perish. (20)
Madhusūdana: By this demonstration of the origin and destruction of those who lack self-control, it has been explained that "the worlds, up to the realm of Brahmā, are subject to return.
Now, with the two verses beginning with "Beyond that," he explains the statement: "Having come to Me, there is no further birth."

Therefore, [the Self] is beyond—that is, distinct from or superior to—the unmanifest (avyakta) known as Hiraṇyagarbha, which is the cause of the gross phenomenal world of moving and non-moving beings; it is the cause even of that [Hiraṇyagarbha].

To the objection that "even if there is distinction, there might still be similarity," he says "no": it is "other," meaning absolutely dissimilar, for the Śruti declares, "There is no likeness of Him.

The Unmanifest is an entity devoid of form and other such qualities, thus beyond the range of the eyes and other senses; it is the reality that persists as the essence of "Being" (sat) throughout all imagined effects.
Therefore, it is eternal and constant.
The word "tu" (but) indicates the distinction of this eternal unmanifest from the discardable, non-eternal unmanifest, signifying its quality as something to be accepted.
The meaning is that such a being, like Hiraṇyagarbha, does not perish even when all beings perish, nor is it born even when they are born.

The meaning is this: since Hiraṇyagarbha is the presiding deity (abhimānin) over the elements that constitute his effect, he is indeed subject to origination and destruction through the origination and destruction of those elements; however, this does not apply to the Supreme Lord (parameśvara), who is not such a presiding deity and is not a mere effect. //20//
Viśvanātha: Therefore, [the Lord] is superior—that is, more excellent—than the unmanifest Prajāpati Hiraṇyagarbha, who possesses the characteristics previously described;
for He is indeed another unmanifest state (avyakta-bhāva), eternal and beginningless, who is the cause even of Hiraṇyagarbha. //20//

Baladeva: Thus, by showing the birth and destruction of those governed by the system of karma, [the Lord] has explained this [state] "up to the world of Brahmā. Now, He explains this [higher state] by saying "beyond that" (*tasmāt paraḥ*) with reference to Me. The meaning is: that entity or reality which is other than—that is, superior to and entirely distinct from—that unmanifest Brahman who is Hiraṇyagarbha; that is the object of worship.

He states the extreme distinctiveness [of the Self] with the word "unmanifest" (*avyakta*). The meaning is that it is "direct" (*pratyak*) because its form is the Self (*ātman*). However, it was stated previously that when [the mind] is purified, it also becomes perceptible (*pratyakṣa*).
It is eternal and beginningless; indeed, it does not perish even when all beings, down to Hiraṇyagarbha, have perished. //20//
That which is called the unmanifest and the imperishable is said to be the supreme goal; having attained that, they do not return—that is my supreme abode. 8.21
Śrīdhara, demonstrating the proof for its imperishability, says:
"The unmanifest," meaning that entity which is unmanifest and beyond the senses;
"the indestructible," meaning devoid of entering or perishing.

Thus, in such scriptural passages as "From the Imperishable (akṣara) the universe arises here," He is called the "Imperishable. They declare Him to be the supreme goal, the object to be attained, and the ultimate human purpose.
Scriptural texts such as "There is nothing higher than the Person; that is the culmination, that is the supreme goal" [establish this].
He states that this is indeed the supreme goal by saying, "having reached which they do not return.
And that is my very abode, my own essential nature (*svarūpa*).
The genitive case in the word "mama" (my) is used in a figurative sense (*upacāre*).
It is like the expression "the head of Rāhu.
Therefore, the meaning is: "I alone am the supreme goal. //21//

Madhusūdana: That state which is here called the "unmanifest" and the "imperishable," and which is likewise described in other Śrutis and Smṛtis as that state regarding which the Śrutis and Smṛtis say, "There is nothing higher than the Puruṣa;
that is the limit, that is the supreme goal," and so forth—[that is the state].
It is the supreme goal, consisting of the nature of supreme bliss and self-luminosity, devoid of birth and destruction, and resting in the ultimate purpose of man (puruṣārtha).
That state which, once attained, they do not return from to further worldly existence—that abode is my own essential nature, Viṣṇu’s supreme and most excellent.
The use of the genitive case in "my abode" (*mama dhāma*) is a conceptual distinction, like the expression "the head of Rāhu.
Therefore, the meaning is that I alone am the supreme goal. //21//
Viśvanātha: He explains the word "unmanifest" (avyakta), which was mentioned in the preceding verse, as follows: "The Unmanifest.

[It is called] the Imperishable (akṣara) because it does not decay; it is Nārāyaṇa. For the Śruti says: "In the beginning there was only one Nārāyaṇa; there was neither Brahmā nor Śaṅkara. It is my supreme abode, my eternal essential nature.
Or rather, the Imperishable is the supreme abode; it is Brahman itself, which is my abode and whose nature consists of my splendor. //21//

Baladeva: That entity which is here called "the unmanifest" and "the imperishable," the Vedāntas declare to be the supreme goal, stating at the outset: "There is nothing higher than the Puruṣa; that is the limit, that is the supreme goal.
Having attained and reached that entity, people do not return—they do not undergo rebirth—and that entity is indeed myself; thus he says, "That."
Therefore, this sixth [consciousness] should be understood as my own abode, my supreme and glorious essential nature, just as it is said that consciousness is the essential nature of the Self. //21//
That Supreme Person, O Pārtha, is attainable by unswerving devotion alone— He within whom all beings dwell and by whom all this is pervaded. 8.22

Śrīdhara: It has already been stated that devotion is the internal means for attaining Him; thus he says, "The Supreme Person. And He—meaning I, the Supreme Person—is attainable only by unswerving devotion (*ananya-bhakti*), which is that in which no other [refuge] exists as its object. It is attained solely through such exclusive devotion.
It is not otherwise;
he declares his very supremacy: within the midst of whom, who has become the cause, all beings abide, and by whom, who has become the cause, this entire world is stretched out and pervaded. //22//

Madhusūdana: Previously it was stated, "I am easily attained by him who constantly remembers Me at all times with undivided mind. Now, He declares that very yoga of devotion as the means for attaining Him, beginning with the words "That Person...":

"That Supreme Person"—the unsurpassed Person, the Supreme Self, who is indeed Myself—is attainable only through unswerving devotion, characterized by love, wherein no other object exists; not otherwise.
In response to the inquiry "Who is he?", he says: that Person within whom all beings—that is, all effects—reside, because an effect resides within its cause;
for this very reason, by that Person all this multitude of effects is stretched out and pervaded.
There is nothing else superior to him, nor anything smaller or greater than he.
The one remains fixed like a tree in heaven; by that Puruṣa all this is filled.
Whatever exists in the entire world—whether it is seen or even heard—Nārāyaṇa stands pervading all of that, both within and without.
And because of scriptural passages such as, "He has pervaded all, the Pure One," and so forth. //22//
Viśvanātha: And He is the Supreme Person, a portion of Me.
By that very [devotion] in which no other action, yoga, desire, or the like exists;
for this reason, the sense is that I previously stated, "with a mind focused on nothing else, constantly" (ananyacetāḥ satatam). //22//

Baladeva: He states that devotion is an excellent means for attaining Him in the verse beginning with "That Person. That Person, characterized as Me, is to be attained—capable of being reached—by devotion alone, as previously described, which is constant and characterized by a mind focused on nothing else but Him; the meaning is that through the devotion of yoga, His attainment is difficult to achieve.
He states its definition with the words "of which":
by which all this world is stretched out, that is, pervaded.
And the Śruti says thus:
The one, self-controlled, all-pervading Kṛṣṇa is worthy of praise;
though being one, he appears as many.
Like a tree, he stands firm and alone in heaven.
"Therefore, all this is filled by the Puruṣa," and so forth. //22//
I shall now describe that time, O bull of the Bharatas, at which departing yogis go either to non-return or to return. 8.23
Śrīdhara: Thus, it has been stated that those who worship the Supreme Lord, having attained His state, do not return, whereas others do return.
In that regard, by which path do those who have gone not return?

In response to the inquiry, "By what [path] do they go and by what do they return?", he says, "Wherein" (yatra). The syntactical connection is as follows: I shall declare that time—at which time those who have departed reach non-return, and at which time those who have departed reach return.

And here, by the principle indicated in the aphorisms "following the rays" and "even during the southern course," since death at specific times such as the northern course is not intended [as a restrictive factor], the word "time" (kāla) indicates the path to be reached by the presiding deities of time (kālābhimāninī), who are of a superphysical nature (ātivāhikī).
Therefore, this is the meaning: on whichever path characterized by the presiding deities of time the yogins, worshippers, and ritualists depart, they go respectively to non-return or to return.

"I shall describe that path characterized by the deity presiding over time (kālābhimānin). Although Agni and Jyotis lack the status of being deities presiding over time, since the majority of those denoted by terms such as "day" (ahar) and so forth do possess the status of deities presiding over time, it is not contradictory to characterize them by the word "time" (kāla) through association with those [deities], just as one speaks of an "orchard of mango trees" (āmra-vana) and the like. //23//
Madhusūdana: Those who worship Brahman with attributes (saguṇa-brahma) do not return even after reaching His state, but rather attain liberation gradually.

In that regard, for those who have not yet attained perfect realization (samyag-darśana) prior to enjoying that world, there exists a dependence upon a path; however, this dependence does not exist for those who possess perfect realization. Thus, the path of the gods (devayāna-mārga) is taught for the sake of the worshippers' attainment of that world.
The presentation of the path of the fathers (*pitṛ-yāna*), however, is for the purpose of praising that [other path],

wherein— immediately after the departure of the vital breaths— at which time and on which path characterized by the deities presiding over time, yogins, meditators, and ritualists go either to non-return or to return;
and ritualists who have set out on the path of the gods (*deva-yāna*) go to return.

Although it has been stated—even in the case of those who have set out on the path of the gods—that they return, as in the passage, "All worlds up to the realm of Brahmā are subject to return," nevertheless, those who have gone by the path of the ancestors (pitṛ-yāna) certainly do return; no one there attains gradual liberation (krama-mukti).
However, among those who have gone by the path of the gods, although some who meditate on symbols (pratīkopāsaka) return, [others go] as far as the world of lightning.

Even those who worship the knowledge of the five fires (*pañcāgni-vidyā*) and so forth—though led by the superhuman being (*amānava-puruṣa*) as far as Hiraṇyagarbha—are indeed subject to return at the end of their enjoyment because they lack that specific resolve (*atat-kratu*). Nevertheless, those who worship the "small [space]" (*dahara*) and others are liberated gradually;
thus, it is not the case that all of them return at the end of their enjoyment.
Therefore, the path of the fathers (pitṛ-yāna) is inferior because its fruit is necessarily characterized by return; however,
this path of the gods (deva-yāna) is highly praised because its fruit is non-return, for even in the case of some who do return, the quality of having non-return as the ultimate fruit remains intact.
I shall describe that path of the gods and the path of the ancestors— the path characterized by Time (kāla) and the deities presiding over Time—

O bull of the Bharatas. In this context, if the word "Time" (kāla) is taken in its primary sense, then the application of the words "fire," "light," "smoke," "going" (gati), and "moving" (sṛti) becomes appropriate.

And thus, in accordance with that [principle], a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is resorted to in the single word "time" (*kāla*), because deities presiding over time abound in both paths. Just as the term *agnihotra* serves as an indicator by means of a single part even when fire and smoke—the two other factors—are present, so too is the word "time" an indicator by means of a single part.
Otherwise, since the deity Agni would be absent in the morning, there would be the rule: "And another scriptural passage [establishes it] by its resemblance to that" (*Mīmāṃsā-sūtra* 1.4.4).
By this [statement], it would not be [appropriate] as a designation for Him.
Furthermore, "a grove of mango trees" (*āmra-vana*) is a worldly example.
Viśvanātha says: "But surely, by Your own statement, 'That is My supreme abode, reaching which they do not return,' it has been said that Your devotees, having reached You, do not return again."

It has been stated that there is no fixed rule regarding the path for those who do not abide in You. Furthermore, because Your devotees have transcended the qualities (guṇas), their path is also determined to be one that transcends the qualities;
it is not the sāttvika path consisting of the arcis and so forth.

In response to the expectation, "I wish to know that path which belongs to the yogin, the man of knowledge, and the performer of action," he says, "Where... The syntactical connection is as follows: I shall describe that time and that path, upon which those who have departed after the departure of the vital breath reach either non-return or return, characterized by that specific time. 23.
Baladeva: The return of His devotees has been stated, as well as the return of those who are averse to Him.
In response to the inquiry as to by which path those [who return] have gone, He says "where" (yatra).
This refers to yogis, devotees, and those who perform actions with desire for rewards.

Here, by the word "Time" (kāla), the deities presiding over time are meant. Since fire and smoke themselves are not time, they are referred to by the word "Time" because the terms *mahat* and so forth, as well as the terms *rātri* and so forth, frequently denote time; thus, it should be understood that the path protected by the deities of the "light" (*arcis*) and so forth, and the "smoke" (*dhūma*) and so forth, is designated by the word "Time. //23//
Fire, light, day, the bright fortnight, and the six months of the northern solstice— departing there, those people who know Brahman go to Brahman. 8.24

Śrīdhara: In that regard, he states the path of non-return with the words "Agni" and so forth. By the words "fire" (agni) and "light" (jyotis), the deity presiding over the "rays" (arciḥ)—as mentioned in the Śruti passage "they attain the rays"—is indicated. "Day" (ahar) refers to the deity presiding over the day.

"Śuklā" (the Bright One) is the presiding deity of the bright fortnight; "the six months of the northern course" is the presiding deity of the northern course. This is intended as an illustration for other deities mentioned in the Śruti, such as the Year, the World of the Gods, and so forth.

Those people who are devotees of the Blessed One and have set out upon that path which is of such a nature attain Brahman, because they are knowers of Brahman. And thus says the Śruti: "They pass into the light; from the light into day, from day into the waxing fortnight, from the waxing fortnight into those six months during which the sun moves northward, and from the months into the world of the gods."
Thus it is said:
for those who partake in immediate liberation and are established in right vision, there is no movement anywhere, nor do their vital breaths depart. //24//

Madhusūdana says: In that context, he describes for the worshippers the path called the "devayāna" (the path of the gods) with the words beginning with "Agni. By "Agni, light," the deity presiding over the *arcis* (flame) is indicated; by "day," the deity presiding over the day; by "bright fortnight," the deity presiding over the bright fortnight; and by "six months of the northern course," [the deity presiding over] the six months of the northern solstice.

Thus, by the principle stated in *Brahma Sūtra* 4.3.4—"The deities presiding over the six months of the northern course are indicated as the conductors, because of the indicative marks"—it is precisely the deity presiding over the six-month period of the northern solstice who is intended.
This is also for the purpose of indicating other deities mentioned in the Śruti.
Accordingly, the Śruti says: "They reach the light (*arciḥ*); from the light, to the day; from the day, to the waxing fortnight..."

Those who go by the six-month path [attain] from the months to the year, from the year to the sun, from the sun to the moon, and from the moon to lightning. There a person who is not human dwells; he leads them to Brahman. This is the path of the gods, the path of Brahman.
Those who proceed by this do not return to this human whirlpool.

In this regard, in accordance with another scriptural passage, it has been determined in the authoritative treatises that after the year comes the deity of the world of the gods, then the deity Vāyu, and then Āditya;
likewise, after lightning come Varuṇa, Indra, and Prajāpati, at which point the stages of the path are completed.
Among those, the deities of the flame, the day, the bright fortnight, and the northern solstice have been mentioned here.
The year, the world of the gods, Vāyu, Āditya, Candramas, Vidyut, Varuṇa, Indra, and Prajāpati—these, though not explicitly mentioned, are also to be understood [as stages on the path].

There, those who have set out upon the path of the gods proceed toward Brahman that is conditioned by its effects (*kārya*), according to the principle: "Bādari [holds that they go] to the effected Brahman, because of the logical possibility of such a journey" (VS 4.3.7). However, it is through that very door that they attain the unconditioned Brahman, as this results in liberation by successive stages (*krama-mukti*).
The "knowers of Brahman" (brahma-vidas) are those people who worship the Saguna-Brahman.
Regarding the scriptural statement, "Those proceeding by this [path] do not return to this human whirlpool," the qualification "this" (imam) implies that some may return during another cycle (kalpa).
For this very reason, the Blessed One has remained neutral here, as he has already provided an explanation through the description of the scriptural path itself. //24//
Viśvanātha: Here, he describes the path of non-return by saying "Agni" and so forth.

By the scriptural statement, "By means of the words Agni and Jyotis, they attain the *arciḥ*," the deity presiding over the *arciḥ* (the flame) is indicated. "Day" refers to the deity presiding over the day.

"Śukla" refers to the presiding deity of the bright fortnight; "the six months of the northern course" refers to the deity who presides over the northern course. Those knowers of Brahman, the wise, who set out upon the path of this nature, attain Brahman.

And so says the Śruti: "They attain the light; from the light, to the day; from the day, to the waxing fortnight; from the waxing fortnight, to those six months during which the sun moves northward; from the months, to the world of the gods. //24//
Baladeva: Regarding that, he states the path of non-return with the words "Agni" and so forth.

By the terms *agni* (fire) and *jyotis* (light), the deity presiding over the *arciḥ* (flame) mentioned in the Śruti is indicated. By *ahaḥ* (day), the deity presiding over the day is indicated; by *śuklaḥ* (the bright), the deity presiding over the bright fortnight is indicated.
"Six months" refers to the northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*); thus, [the text] speaks of one who identifies with the northern course consisting of six months.
And this is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for other periods mentioned in the Śruti, such as the year and so forth.
The Chāndogyas recite: "Now, whether they perform funeral rites for him here or not, they certainly proceed to the light (*arciḥ*)."
From the rays [of light] they go to the day; from the day to the waxing fortnight; from the waxing fortnight to those six months during which the sun moves northward;
from those months to the year; from the year to the sun; from the sun to the moon; from the moon to the lightning.
There is a person who is not human; he leads them to Brahman. This is the path of the gods, the path to Brahman; those who proceed by this path do not return to the cycle of rebirth.
"Let them not return to this whirlpool of human existence.

(4.15.5) The meaning of this is as follows: when this group of worshippers of Brahman residing in the eye has died, whether their sons, disciples, and others perform the funeral rites—such as cremation and so forth—connected with the corpse (*śava*), or whether they do not perform them; [in either case, they do not return].
In both cases, those worshippers, whose fruit of worship remains unimpaired, proceed by way of the deities beginning with Light (arcis) to that which is to be worshipped; this other point is clear.
Here, the world of Vāyu should be inserted between the Year and the Sun.
Beyond the Lightning, Varuṇa, Indra, and Prajāpati are to be understood in succession.
The detailed explanation is found in the authoritative texts (*ākara*) based on other Vedic scriptures (*śruti*).

The author of the Sūtras states: "These [beings] are conducting deities (*ātivāhika*), because of the indicative mark thereof" (VS 4.3.4). This refers to the non-human, eternal attendants of the Supreme Lord Hari, who are the deities known as Arcis and the others.

Thus, by the path served by twelve deities beginning with *arciḥ* (light) who abide by the command of the Blessed One, the devotees of the Blessed One proceed to the Blessed One and do not return from there;
so it has been stated by the authorities:
"By the light, the day, the bright fortnight, the northward course of the sun here, the autumn, the wind, and the sun..."
"By means of the Moon, Lightning, Varuṇa, Indra, and Brahmā, the liberated one attains the abode of Hari. //24//
Smoke, night, as well as the dark fortnight and the six months of the sun's southern course— attaining the lunar light during that time, the yogin returns. (8.25)
Śrīdhara says: He describes the path of return with the words "smoke" (*dhūma*).
"Smoke" refers to the deity who presides over smoke.
And by the words "night" (*rātri*) and so forth, as before, three deities presiding over the night, the dark fortnight, and the six months of the sun's southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*) are indicated.

The path characterized by these deities is that which the practitioner of action (karma-yogin) has traveled; having reached the lunar light—that is, the heavenly world characterized by it—and having there enjoyed the fruits of his performed sacrifices and charitable works (iṣṭāpūrta), he returns again.
Regarding this, the Śruti says: "They pass into smoke; from smoke, into night; from night, into the waning fortnight."

"During those six months when the sun moves southward from the waning fortnight, they go from the world of men to the world of the fathers, and from the world of the fathers to the moon; having reached the moon, they become food.

Thus, through meditation accompanied by works of cessation (*nivṛtti-karman*), there is gradual liberation (*krama-mukti*); whereas through works performed for desire (*kāmya-karman*), there is a return after the enjoyment of heaven.
However, for those who perform prohibited actions, there is a return [to this world] immediately after experiencing the hells;
but for creatures who perform trivial actions, it should be understood that they take birth again and again right here on earth. //25//
Madhusūdana: In order to praise the path of the gods (devayānamārga), [the text] speaks of the path of the ancestors (pitṛyānamārga) beginning with "smoke.

Here too, "smoke" refers to the deity presiding over smoke; "night" refers to the deity presiding over night; "the dark fortnight" refers to the deity presiding over the dark fortnight; and "the six months of the southern progress" indicates the deity presiding over the southern progress. This also serves as an illustration for the other deities mentioned in the Śruti.

For thus says the Śruti: "They pass into smoke; from smoke, into night; from night, into the waning fortnight; from the waning fortnight, they go to those six months when the sun moves southward. They do not reach the year from those months; rather, from the months they reach the world of the fathers (pitṛloka);
from the world of the fathers, into space; from space, into the moon. That is King Soma, the food of the gods; that the gods consume."
"Having dwelt there until the exhaustion [of their merit], they then return again by this very same path.

In that regard, having set out upon that path, the yogi—the practitioner of karma-yoga who performs sacrifices, pious works, and acts of charity—attains the lunar light as his fruit; having dwelt there until the exhaustion of his merit, he returns.
That by which one falls back is "sampāta," meaning karma;
therefore, the meaning is that the path of non-return is superior to this path of return. //25//
Viśvanātha: [The text] states the path of return for those who perform ritual actions (karmiṇaḥ) with the words "smoke" (dhūmaḥ) and so forth. "Smoke" refers to the deity presiding over smoke.
And by the words "night" (rātri) and the rest, as before, three deities presiding over those respective things are indicated.

The practitioner of action (karma-yogin), having set out upon that path characterized by these deities and having reached the lunar light—that is, the heavenly world characterized by it—enjoys the fruit of his actions and returns. //25//
Baladeva: Now he describes the path of non-return with the words, "smoke, night," and so forth.
There too, as before, the presiding deities (abhimānin-devas) of smoke, night, the dark fortnight, and the six months of the southern solstice (dakṣiṇāyana) are to be understood.
This is an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa) for the year, the world of the ancestors (pitṛloka), space (ākāśa), and the moon, which are mentioned in the Śruti.
The Chāndogyas recite: "Now, those here in the village who worship with the thought, 'Sacrifices, works of public utility, and gifts,' they pass into smoke;
from smoke into night; from night into the waning half of the month; from the waning half of the month into the six months during which the sun moves southward—these do not reach the year."

"From the months [they go] to the world of the fathers; from the world of the fathers to space; from space to the moon. That King Soma is the food of the gods; the gods consume him. Having dwelt there for as long as the residue of their works lasts, they then return again by this very same path. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.3–5). Thus, by the path protected by the eight deities—such as Dhūma and others—who abide by the command of the Supreme Lord, those who perform rites for desired fruits reach the lunar world, and upon the exhaustion of their enjoyment, they return from there once more.
Thus [ends the twenty-fifth].
These two paths of the world, the bright and the dark, are considered eternal.
By the one, a person goes to non-return; by the other, he returns again. (8.26)
Śrīdhara concludes by stating "the two paths" with the words "śukla... (white, etc.).

The path beginning with the white radiance (*śuklārcir-ādi-gati*) consists of light because it is composed of illumination; the path beginning with smoke (*kṛṣṇā dhūmādi-gati*) consists of darkness because it is composed of obscurity.
These two paths, these two ways, are held to be eternal—meaning beginningless—for the world that is qualified for knowledge and action, since *saṃsāra* itself is beginningless.
Of these two, by the white one he goes to non-return, which is liberation; but by the other, the black one, he returns again. //26//

Madhusūdana concludes the two paths mentioned with the words "the bright and the dark. The path beginning with the bright flame consists of the nature of the light of knowledge; the dark path beginning with smoke consists of the nature of darkness due to the absence of knowledge.
These two paths of white and black are indeed well-known as the destinies for those qualified for knowledge and action accompanied by the qualities (*guṇas*).
They are considered eternal and beginningless for the entire world, including those who know the scriptures, because *saṃsāra* itself is beginningless.
By one of these, the white path, someone goes to a state from which there is no return.
By means of another [mantra] consisting of the syllable Kṛṣṇa, everyone returns once again. //26//
Viśvanātha: He concludes the two paths mentioned by saying "the white and the black.
They are eternal (*śāśvate*), meaning beginningless, because *saṃsāra* is beginningless.
By the one, the white path, there is no return—that is, liberation; but by the other, the black path, one is born here again and again. (26)
Baladeva: He summarizes the two paths mentioned with the word "śukla" (white).
The path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi*) is white because it consists of luminosity; the path beginning with smoke (*dhūmādi*) is black because it is devoid of luminosity.
These are the paths; those who have traveled them—those entitled to knowledge and ritual action—are [destined for] the eternal, beginningless world, for that [world] is beginningless.
The rest is clear. //26//
O Pārtha, no yogin who knows these two paths is ever deluded.
Therefore, O Arjuna, at all times remain disciplined in yoga. 8.27
Śrīdhara: Demonstrating a portion of the knowledge of the path, he concludes the discourse on *bhakti-yoga* with the words "Not these.
Knowing these two paths—that which leads to liberation and that which leads to worldly existence—no yogi whatsoever is deluded;
he does not desire results such as heaven out of a sense of pleasure.
However, the meaning is that one becomes solely devoted to the Supreme Lord;
the rest is clear. //27//
Madhusūdana: [The Lord] praises the knowledge of those two paths so that the path may be worthy of meditation, saying "Not these...

O Pārtha, the yogi established in meditation, discerning that "these two paths"—one for gradual liberation and the other for rebirth—does not become deluded; he simply does not regard as something to be performed the action that leads to the path of smoke and so forth.
"Anyone at all"—that is, whoever.
Therefore, because yoga has the fruit of non-return, be disciplined in yoga with a concentrated mind at all times for the sake of non-return, O Arjuna! (27)
Viśvanātha: This knowledge of the two paths generates discernment; therefore, he praises one who possesses it with the words "Not these... [and so forth].
Be disciplined in yoga, with a concentrated mind. (27)
Baladeva: [The Lord] praises that knowledge of these two paths because it is the cause of discrimination, saying "naite... (these two...).

Knowing the two paths—the path beginning with light for liberation and the path beginning with smoke for worldly existence—and remembering them, no yogi who is My devotee is deluded; the meaning is that he does not determine, as something to be performed, the action that leads to the path of smoke and so forth.
Being disciplined in yoga and established in samādhi, one attains the state from which there is no return. //27//
Whatever meritorious fruit there is in the Vedas, in sacrifices, in austerities, and indeed in acts of charity;
Having understood all this, the yogin transcends it all and attains the supreme, primordial state. //28//
Śrīdhara concludes the purpose of the chapter—the determination of the meaning of the eight questions—along with its fruit, in the verse beginning with "In the Vedas" (vedeṣu):
"In the Vedas" by means of study and so forth;
"in sacrifices" by means of performance and so forth.

Whatever fruit of merit is taught in the scriptures through ascetic practices such as the emaciation of the body, and through acts of giving such as the offering to worthy recipients— all that he transcends.
Even beyond that, he attains the sovereignty of yoga.
Having done what? Having known this reality (tattva) as declared through the determination of the meaning of the eight questions.
And then, having become a knower through yoga, he attains the supreme, most excellent, primordial station of Viṣṇu—the source of the universe, the highest abode. //28//
In the eighth [chapter], which is distinguished by eight [sections] and the determination of eight interconnected meanings,
the attainment of the desired state is clearly explained by means of the supreme path.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Yoga of the Tāraka Brahman," in the *Subodhinī*, a commentary on the *Bhagavad-gītā* composed by the venerable Śrīdhara Svāmī.
Madhusūdana: Again, for the sake of increasing faith, He praises Yoga with the words "In the Vedas" (*vedeṣu*).
This refers to when the Vedas have been properly studied through such means as holding *darbha* grass as a purifier in the hand, facing the east, and remaining under the guidance of a teacher;
and when sacrifices have been properly performed with faith, accompanied by their primary and secondary limbs (*aṅga-upāṅga*).

Having understood all this— which has been explained by way of answering the seven previously mentioned questions— and having ascertained it as culminating in right practice, the yogi established in meditation transcends all that merit and fruit of merit (dharma)— such as heaven, sovereignty, and so forth— prescribed in the scriptures as the fruit of well-performed austerities taught in the scriptures through faith and one-pointedness of mind, intellect, and other faculties, and of gifts such as the *tulā-puruṣa* given properly with faith at the right place, time, and to a worthy recipient. He transcends all that.

It does not merely transcend that [state], but rather attains and reaches the supreme, most excellent, sovereign station—the primordial cause of all; the meaning is that it attains Brahman itself, the cause of all.
Thus, by this chapter, the referent of the word "That" (tat-pada-artha) has been explained as the object of meditation. //28//

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Imperishable Supreme Brahman according to the Distinction of Qualifications," in the *Śrīmad-Bhagavad-Gītā-Gūḍhārtha-Dīpikā* (The Lamp Illuminating the Hidden Meaning of the Śrīmad-Bhagavad-Gītā) composed by the venerable Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, disciple of the feet of the venerable Viśveśvara Sarasvatī, the wandering ascetic teacher (*parivrājaka-ācārya*) of the illustrious Paramahaṃsa order.
Viśvanātha: He states the fruit of knowing the subject matter taught in this chapter with the words "In the Vedas...
The yogi endowed with devotion transcends all that—that is, having passed beyond it—and attains even a higher state than that: the primordial, non-material, and eternal abode. //28//

The preeminence of devotees in every respect was previously stated by You; now, in this chapter, the meaning that it pertains specifically to the *ananya-bhakta* (the exclusive devotee) has been clearly manifested.

Thus, in this delightful commentary *Sārārthavarṣiṇī*, which showers the essential meaning for the hearts of devotees, the eighth chapter of the Śrī Gītā has been appropriately concluded for the virtuous. 8.
Baladeva states the method of knowledge through the two chapters, the seventh and the eighth, beginning with the words "In the Vedas" (*vedeṣu*).
This refers to when the Vedas have been properly studied according to the rules of celibacy and service to the guru; when [the Vedic injunctions] have been properly performed in their entirety;
and when austerities (*tapas*) have been correctly practiced according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures.

Whatever fruit of merit characterized by heavenly realms, sovereignty, and so forth has been declared and taught for gifts properly bestowed with faith after examining the place, time, and recipient—that entire [fruit] he approaches and surpasses.
Having done what? He says: "this."

The meaning is this: having understood through the company of the virtuous the majesty of Me, the Blessed One, and of My devotee as described in these two chapters, the yogi regards all that—beyond the bliss of such knowledge—as mere straw. Thereafter, becoming a devotee of Mine, he attains My primordial, beginningless, and supreme abode which transcends Māyā. //28//
The person who is a portion of Kṛṣṇa is attainable through yoga and devotion by means of the path beginning with light;
however, Kṛṣṇa Himself is attainable only through exclusive devotion—this is the conclusion of the eighth [chapter].
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the commentary on the Śrīmad-Bhagavad-gītā Upaniṣad.
